en: Preface to the *Zhengguan ji* (Record of Correct Contemplation), a Commentary on the Meaning of the *Sūtra of Contemplation*.
The Great Wisdom Patriarch of Lingzhi flourished during the Five Hundred-Year Cycle in the Song Dynasty.

Having extensively investigated the various schools, he took the Vinaya as his fundamental principle and propagated the *Dharmaguptaka-vinaya* by embodying the perfect intent of the *Lotus Sūtra*. Thus, he caused the teachings of the Zhongnan tradition to flourish tenfold.

The brilliance of his achievements and virtue is that which all scholars of the world look up to with reverence; it is not an exaggeration to say that he was like the single fox-fur cloak of a Song dynasty monk.
Beyond his propagation of the Vinaya, he cultivated the practice of the Pure Land for himself and transformed others through it;

thus, he composed commentaries on both the *Sixteen Contemplations* and the *Shorter Amitābha Sūtra*. Compared to those of other masters, these are not without points of agreement and difference, as each...

It was necessary to adapt to the capacities of sentient beings; thus, it could not have been otherwise. Those who followed and transmitted his legacy were all eminent figures, yet only Vinaya Master Duanzhu (Zhu’an) is hailed as particularly outstanding.
He once assisted in the compilation of the *Zhengguan ji* for the *Amitābha Sūtra Commentary* and the *Wenchi ji* for the *Meditation Sutra Commentary*.
While the *Wenchi ji* has long been transmitted in this land, the *Zhengguan ji* has not yet circulated, which remains a regret for scholars.
The Dharma Master Dayun Run, the abbot of Dewang Monastery on Mount Tiantai, is also an outstanding member of this school.
Recently, he obtained this manuscript at the sutra repository of Chōryū-ji Temple in Nō and intended to have it carved into woodblocks to facilitate its widespread circulation;
thus, he requested a preface from me. Although I am humble and unskilled in composition, I am deeply delighted that this book, which had long been hidden, has now been recovered.

How could Xian possibly refuse such a request? Students who attain the commentaries through the sub-commentaries, and who, by means of the sub-commentaries, penetrate the scriptural teachings to establish their practice—such that they can accord with principle and transcend the mundane and the sacred in this very moment, and dissolve the distinction between the pure and the defiled within a single mind—will have no cause for shame before Śāriputra during their lifetime, and will have no error regarding rebirth in the Lotus Land after death. This is the preface.
In the sixth year of the Bōei cycle, the year of Jichou (1709), on the day of the full moon in the second month of spring,
the junior monk Hyesuk, of the An’gong Hermitage at Donghu, bathed himself in incense and water and respectfully inscribed this with a prostration.
*Record of Right Contemplation: A Commentary on the Meaning of the Sūtra of the Vision of the Divine Mushroom* (Volume One), including the preface.
Composed by the Śramaṇa Jièdù of Zúān at Lóngshān in Sìmíng.
The Buddhas of the ten directions praise Amitābha with one voice; all sentient beings who maintain their resolve rejoice together.
The Land of Peaceful Nurturing (An-yang) arose from the Ocean of Forty-eight Vows of the Dharma Treasury (Dharmākara), which is peerless and beyond compare;
Śākyamuni expounded the sixteen Contemplation Gates (ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā-mukha), which constitute the most sublime practice, benefiting those of both sharp and dull faculties.

Whether through the cultivation of principle or phenomena, all are the primary causes for the nine grades of rebirth, and all gather as noble companions on the path of the Three Vehicles (triyāna). Through successive translations spanning many generations and the continuous emergence of commentaries, these teachings have become like gold and jade.

Vying in brilliance like orchids and chrysanthemums, each excels in literary beauty, richness of meaning, and breadth of principle; they truly yield to their predecessors, making the manifest truths clear and distinct, such that no contemporary commentary can equal them.

Thus, the entry into the Way is distinguished between the two lands, and the capacity for exposition is judged across the generations; as the pure and the mixed are now separated, the source and its stream do not become confused.
If one examines the discourses of antiquity, one may test how they rejected the erroneous to follow the correct and eliminated the spurious to transmit the true.

Furthermore, these matters cannot be discussed on the same footing; for while a "night-light" jewel truly pales in comparison when cast into the darkness, the song of falling snow is difficult for vulgar ears to hear.
To follow my impulses and deceive others, or to trust my pen to disparage and revile, may resolve the disputes of the multitude, yet the true refinement of our culture remains obstructed.
Whenever I reflect upon this, I feel deep remorse in my heart; therefore, I have ventured to compose these clumsy words and dare to call them a work.

The author has gathered the hearsay and insights of former sages to serve as a fishing trap for later students. May they not be deluded by heterodox paths but strive to cultivate the Right Contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), suddenly realizing that this very mind is Buddha.
Let us together aspire to be reborn in the highest grade of the Upper Realm; though the great void may be fathomed, this mind is boundless.
Written on the day of the summer retreat in the eighth year of the Chunxi era, the year of Xinchou, while residing at Jie Temple on the southern lake.
The preface to the commentary states:
Regarding the titles within the headings, the initial explanation of the title of the sutra is as follows; the commentary itself provides its own interpretation.

Alternatively, one may apply the various analytical methods—such as those concerning the agent and the object, the general and the specific, or the Chinese and Sanskrit designations—as appropriate. Here, I shall not elaborate further on these points, as they are intended for the *Yishu* (Explanatory Commentary). "Yi" (義) refers to the meaning.

It is because he has also pre-emptively extracted the profound meanings of the sutras and extensively cited the sacred teachings of the Tripiṭaka to expound their essential principles, thereby perfectly harmonizing with the capacities and needs of his audience.
"Shu" (Commentary) means to clear away; it refers to clearing away doubts and obstructions so that, by examining the text, one perceives the meaning clearly and transparently.

Thus, the title of the commentary is used concurrently as the heading for the preface and the notes to demonstrate this. The remainder is as explained in the usual interpretations. The author’s name is given in both Chinese and Western (Sanskrit) style.
Hulu is located to the west of the city of Qiantang Prefecture; it is truly one of the finest scenic sites under heaven. A temple stands in its midst.
In the past, within the gardens of the Qian family, purple *zhī* fungi once grew, and they were donated to establish this Buddhist shrine; thus, it was called Lingzhi (Numinous Mushroom).

During the Imperial Dynasty, the title was granted based on the original name of the Honglu (Court of State Ceremonial), hence it is now called a "Temple" (*si*). "Shi" is the clan name for those who have left the household life. The author of this preface, Shuzhu, was a native of Qiantang.

His secular surname was Tang, his courtesy name was Zhanru, and his style name was Anrenzi. He resided in the world to transmit the Way, and his magnificent achievements and noble deeds are fully recorded in his stupa inscription and biographies.
He passed away on the first day of the ninth month in the sixth year of the Zhenghe era at the age of sixty-nine;
his years as a monk (śrāmaṇera-avarṣa) were fifty-one. Facing west, he sat upright and passed away. A stupa was erected to inter his entire remains within the monastery.
This preface for the stupa of the Vinaya Master Daizhi, whose posthumous title was Jieguang, erected in the northwest corner during the Xinsi year of the Shaoxing era, was composed by [the author].
In the first section of the introduction, the four lines of the middle-upper portion cite the environments and inhabitants (*āśraya-vastu*) of the two lands to manifest their purity and defilement;

the four lines of the middle-lower portion follow upon the suffering and joy of the two directions to exhort toward aspiration and revulsion; and the four lines of the final portion cite... [the tide].
The scriptures of the sages and commoners serve as authoritative testimony. The first two lines clarify impurity, while the latter two lines clarify purity;

furthermore, the preceding lines clarify the basis (*āśraya*) and the subsequent lines clarify the actual state (*bhūta*). As for "Endurance" (*Sahā*), it is a Sanskrit term also transliterated as *So-ho*.
The *Karunāpuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states: "Because these sentient beings endure the three poisons and afflictions. The *Buddhakṣetra-sūtra* [states likewise].
There are two meanings. The first meaning is the same as above; it was said previously that "if a bodhisattva achieves patience, they can fully endure any harm inflicted by others.

(Considering the intent of the current text, the second meaning is more remote. Because this kalpa is formed by afflictions, sentient beings, lifespan, and mixed karma, it is called a turbid land (*kaṣāya-bhūmi*).
"Different destinies" refers to the three evil paths; thus, the sutra below states, "this turbid and evil place" (referring to the turbid land). "Ground" (*bhūmi*)—

The hells, hungry ghosts, and animals fill [the world], being a vast accumulation of unwholesomeness (referring to the various realms of existence). This is precisely Śākyamuni’s impure land of cohabitation (*sahā-loka*).
As for "Peaceful Nurturing" (*An-yang*), it is sometimes said that all sentient beings are nurtured in peace and happiness;

it is also said that they dwell securely in the secret treasury and nourish the fundamental body of the Dharma (*dharmakāya*). The *Benpin* (Original Chapter) states: "One shall ultimately transcend the impure and go to be born in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing. That land...
Since both the primary and secondary adornments are accomplished through the power of the Vow as a treasury of Dharma, it is said that the Pure Land consists solely of the Mahāyāna.
Since they are pure and excellent companions, it is said that they are "excellent superiors. The *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Small Version) states: "All excellent superiors gather in one place";

this refers precisely to the Pure Land of Shared Residence of Amitābha. Next, regarding the exhortation to loathe [this world] and aspire [to that land], the first two lines urge one to loathe the forest of thorns.

The "womb-prison" refers to the turbid soil atop the fingers; for the land of the dependent retribution within the three realms produces nothing but thorny thickets and forests, hence it is called the "thorn forest.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* states: "Bricks, rubble, thorns, pits, hollows, and mounds. The primary retributions of the six classes of ordinary beings encompass all four modes of birth (*yoni*).
Now, among humans, most are born from the womb; while the child is in the mother's womb, they undergo all manner of suffering.
Therefore it is said: The *Tāiyù Bǎojī jīng* (Sūtra on the Precious Accumulation of the Womb-Prison) states, "Dwelling in the womb is as unpleasant as being in a prison;

one must exert oneself to take leave. This means that one resolutely arouses the will to forever bid farewell to the toil of worldly existence (as Liu Yimin said: "Proudly taking long leave of the celestial palaces").

The following two lines encourage rejoicing in the precious realm and the golden pond, referring to the aforementioned pure land. Since all the external environment (*niśraya-vipāka*) of that land is composed entirely of the hundred jewels, it is so called.

Regarding the "Jeweled Realm," as stated in the sutra, it refers to jeweled trees, jeweled grounds, jeweled ponds, and so forth. The "golden pond" specifically indicates the place where one is conceived upon rebirth;

this belongs to the primary retribution (*sambhogakāya*). The sutra states that there are ponds made of the seven jewels with channels of gold, and beneath these channels, the ground is entirely composed of various colored *vajra* sands.
The *Smaller Sutra* states that the bottom of the ponds is spread exclusively with golden sand.

Therefore it is said that [the Pure Land] is the "Golden Pond" (some say this refers to a pond where golden lotuses grow from aquatic products, but that is incorrect). Tiantai says it is like a lotus flower in the womb-prison and comparable to a jade tree in a thorny forest;

thus, the two lands are discussed in contrast regarding their environment and inhabitants, and their purity and defilement. In the present commentary, the phrase "the spirit of the Dharma is hidden" (*qianshen*):

"spirit" (*shen*) refers to the mental consciousness (*manas*), and "hidden" (*qian*) means that the mind directed toward rebirth is subtle and dense, making it difficult to perceive. Hence it is called "hidden."

Dharma Master Zhaol said: "To submerge the spirit in profound stillness and harmonize its virtue with empty space" is precisely this. (Some say that "submerging the spirit" refers to one who practices contemplation; this is not correct.
Since one ascends [to the Pure Land] upon a single thought, it is called "going directly. Tiantai says: "With right mindfulness, go directly to be born in An-yang.
Among the three citations of evidence, the first two lines cite a sutra: the Tathāgata’s teaching, adapted to the capacities of sentient beings, is like the tide, which never oversteps its limit.
Regarding the "Tidal Sound," the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "He emits the sound of the ocean tide to address specifically those gathered in this assembly.

Regarding the "Partial Praise," the *Ten Doubts Treatise* quotes the *Sūtra on Rebirth According to One’s Vows*, in which the Bodhisattva Puguang asks the Buddha, "World-Honored One, for what reason do you exclusively praise the Western Pure Land and specifically exhort rebirth there?
The Buddha replied, "The minds of sentient beings are largely turbid and chaotic; it is difficult for them to achieve samādhi. He wished to...
It is for this reason that [the Buddha] exhorted exclusive focus on a single object and mindfulness of a single Buddha, praising him alone;

furthermore, it is said that throughout the various holy teachings of the Great Master Śākyamuni’s lifetime of preaching, he consistently encouraged sentient beings to single-mindedly and exclusively mindfully recite the name of Amitābha Buddha to seek rebirth in the Western Land.
It even states that although other Buddha-lands are briefly recommended for rebirth in one or two sutras, they do not compare to this.
As it is said, "In the land of Amitābha Buddha, [the teachings] are admonished everywhere," and so forth.孤山 (Gushan) says:
"The various scriptures stand in solemn array, yet they all specifically praise the Western Pure Land; how profound is their intent!

*Lang-han* refers to the vessel that holds the abundant scriptures, thereby summoning the words of the Buddha (some say that calling the Buddha’s words "precious" and thus naming them *lang-han* is incorrect). The following two lines cite the transmission that those who attain rebirth there are as numerous as the sea-dwelling creatures.
This is the section on "Cessation" (*śamatha*). Nanshan says: To establish one's will with a solemn vow and dwell loftily beyond all worldly burdens is the "Blue Annals" (*qing shi*).

Looking at the *Biographies of Three Generations of Monks* and the *Records of the Pure Land*, these are equivalent to secular historical records. Since ancient times there was no paper or silk; characters were incised upon bamboo after it had been "killed" (treated with fire), and bound with cured leather; thus it is called the "Blue Annals.
This is the first sub-section of the second part, the "Praise," which provides a general narrative of the faculties and teachings; the first two lines concern the faculties.
Since there is no equal teaching, there must also be a distinction in the methods of guidance. "Yè" (掖) means to support or assist. The *Western Metropolis Rhapsody* states:

"In the inner palace, there are the Yèting and Jiāofáng [palaces]. The commentary says: "Yèting is the name of a palace; it is situated at the left and right of the Son of Heaven, like the armpits (*yè*) of the arms.
Today, we speak of establishing teachings and responding to capacities as being like supporting someone from the left and right so that they suffer no danger of falling. This is frequent.

The *Śūraṅgama-samādhi Sūtra* states: "The nature of returning to the source is non-dual, yet there are many gates of skillful means. Alternatively, the following four lines may be listed separately as four distinct practices;
the first line refers to the *Dhāraṇī-saṃgraha*, the *Bhadrakalpika-sūtra*, the *Ghoṣadatta-sūtra*, and others.

Furthermore, the *Biography of the Inconceivable Spiritual Power of Amitābha* records that Nāgārjuna vowed to be reborn in the Pure Land and, in a dream, was moved by a supernatural being who bestowed upon him the mantra for rebirth (and so forth). Next...

Regarding the first point, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states: "Whether by day or by night, one should single-mindedly recite the Name. The *Amitābha Sūtra* (Small Version) speaks of "holding fast to the Name for one day or seven days," and so forth.
Regarding the third point, the *Pratyutpanna Samādhi Sūtra* instructs that one should constantly fix one's thoughts upon the thirty-two marks of Amitābha for ninety days.

Regarding the fourth point, the *Larger Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* mentions "observing the fast and precepts for ten days and ten nights," and so on; each of these refers to the two lower grades [of rebirth].

The concluding verses further briefly illustrate the method of practice; having already cited the four preceding [verses], they are not fully quoted here, as one should refer to the various scriptures for details.
Only the final two verses below offer a formal praise of this present sutra. The first two lines reveal the excellence of right contemplation (*samyag-darśana*), as the sutra below states:

"One who contemplates in this way is said to possess right contemplation. When contemplation is perfected and the principle is revealed, rebirth is certain; thus, by inferring the result from the cause, it is said that one will "certainly proceed" (*niyata-gati*) there.

"Going to" means to arrive at. The Sūtra says: "Having relinquished this body, one is born before the various Buddhas in other worlds and attains the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).

The latter two phrases clarify the benefits: the first phrase clarifies the benefit of extinguishing evil, and the second phrase clarifies the benefit of generating goodness. Regarding the removal of doubt, the Sūtra says: "One will certainly be born in that land; the mind attains freedom from doubt.
Regarding the abandonment of obstacles, the Sūtra says: "It eliminates the heavy offenses of birth and death accumulated over eighty billion kalpas."

Throughout the text, the Buddha proclaims their names, saying, "Purifying karmic obstructions, they shall be born before all Buddhas," and so forth. Regarding those who attain long life and immortality, the *Daben* (Great Text) states:

"One may obtain extreme longevity, with a lifespan and bliss that are inexhaustible. The *Jingtu chuan* (Biographies of the Pure Land) records that the Dharma Master Tánluán of the Qi dynasty heard that the Recluse Táo had obtained the methods for attaining longevity;
he traveled a thousand *lǐ* to seek them out, but Táo [offered him] only ten chapters of the *Xiānjīng* (Cinnabar Scripture).
When the scroll was bestowed upon him, Sengluan was delighted and took it as proof that the arts of the immortals were indeed certain.

Later, while returning to Luoyang, he encountered Bodhidharma and asked him, "In the Way of the Buddha, is there the attainment of longevity? Is it possible to ward off old age and achieve immortality?
Bodhidharma smiled and said, "Longevity and immortality are precisely the Way of our Buddhas; one simply observes non-existence."
The *Sukhāvatīvyūha Sūtra* instructs him, saying: "You may cultivate this; then you shall not be born again within the three realms, nor have any destination among the six paths of rebirth.
Whether fullness or emptiness, waning or waxing, misfortune or fortune, success or failure—none of these can leave their mark upon it.

That which constitutes its lifespan includes the kalpa-stones and the grains of sand in the Ganges; while the number of grains of sand has an end, the measure of this lifespan has no limit. This is my gold.

The arts of the immortals concern longevity and deathlessness. This broad exposition of the transmission and maintenance of the first section begins with four lines that clarify its widespread prevalence throughout ancient and modern times;
the subsequent four lines clarify the early encounter [with this teaching]. "Tracing back through observation" (*lì guān*) means to look back from the present;

as the *Yījīng* says, "trace back by observing the various hexagrams. "Reaching down to" (*dài jí*) refers to the present moment. As for "receiving and reciting," it means merely holding the text and phrases; as for "delighting in hearing," it means desiring to seek out explanations.

Regarding the phrase "humbly following [others]": as described in the *Duānzhǎngshíèrguāng Chàn* (The Repentance of the Twelve Radiant Lights), after descending to the lower altar, I encountered a grave illness and was at a loss as to where I was heading.
It was only then that I began to apply my mind to pure practices, studying this text with such devotion that I could not set it down from my hands.

This text refers to the present scripture; "having no refuge for billions of kalpas" laments the past when one abandoned one's father and fled, while "relying on [this] for future lives" rejoices in the present domain.

The phrase "the place where the mind finds rest" refers to one's remaining lifespan; thus it is called "the remainder of life. This is precisely what the Master of the Commentary (Zongmi) meant when he said:
"For many lifetimes I have borne my virtues in vain and suffered in the depths of samsara; today I cast myself in sincerity, and my heart is graced with salvation.

In the explanation of the ancient accounts, the first two lines clarify that the former masters were specialists in their respective fields, while the subsequent narration shows they do not go beyond [the teachings of] Tiantai, Huiyuan, and Shandao.
There are commentaries circulating in the world that adhere exclusively to their own schools; they are not considered comprehensive or broad-minded.

Thus it is said, "Each honors [their own view]," and the following two lines clarify that later students are left without a guide, as vast and remote as the Milky Way; hence it says, "they do not know where to go. (The *I Ching* says: "When the superior man has a destination, if he goes first he loses his way, but if he goes last he finds it.
This clarifies the present exposition of the arising of sentiments; therein, the first four lines demonstrate the extensive investigation of what to adopt and what to reject, solely because...

The commentaries and treatises of past and present are profound in their sentiment and detailed in their instructions; yet, because they extensively cover principles and teachings, they are ultimately difficult to comprehend.

Therefore, in this current commentary, I take up the brush and pen without valuing prolixity, pointing directly to the core of the scriptures and striving to preserve the path of cultivation and progress.
This is my sole purpose—what else could it be? "Principles and meanings" refers here to the names and the rational趣 (principle-interest) of the holy teachings of the Tripiṭaka.

"Furthermore, 'ancient and modern' refers to having summoned various masters to repeatedly study their commentaries and treatises; thus it is called 'investigating and deliberating' (*cānxiáng*). 'Comparing and matching' refers to weighing and evaluating them;

thus it is called 'examining and collating. 'Selecting' (*zhì*) means to pick out and gather. (The *Preface to the Commentary on Mencius* says: 'Nowadays, various commentators often select [passages] to explain them.

'Superiority and length' describe that which is precise and appropriate; 'weeding and pruning' (*shānchú jiǎnxiē*) describes that which is redundant and cluttered. (The *Preface to the Book of Documents* says: 'Weeding out the profuse and chaotic, and cutting away the frivolous...')"
[Commentary: This indicates that the style of composition follows brevity, which is why there is mention of "pruning and excising.
Others do not see this and claim that I am abandoning the profound teachings of our Tiantai school; their vehement denunciations are truly laughable (as explained in detail in the *Fuxin lun bian*).

Regarding the four phrases following "narrate" (*shu*): they clarify that in humbling oneself and benefiting others, as well as in establishing words and expounding meanings, one follows the established precedents; hence, it says "narrate" (*shu*).

Yet one should not act with contempt or arrogance. The *Xianxiu xuan* (Selections from the Formerly Cultivated) says: "I take my model from those of former cultivation; this is not something for the secular world to wear.
The commentary notes that "those of former cultivation" refers to people of previous generations who cultivated the Way and its Virtue.

The intent of the current sub-commentary (*shu*) is that by following the sutras and practicing according to them, through cultivation one attains contemplation, and as contemplation is perfected, the principle becomes manifest. Having resolved to be reborn [in the Pure Land], it is said: "To unify these has... [the text continues].
The "Principle" (zōng)—a term originating from the *Book of Changes*—is fundamentally correct in its reasoning and thus fully worthy of being relied upon and inherited;

hence it is said to be "bequeathed to future students," expressing the hope for such a legacy (the *Preface to the Book of Documents* states: "May it perhaps provide benefit for the future"). In the demonstration of the literary style, the first sentence clarifies that the teaching differs from the ancient profusion and complexity;

hence it is called "simple and easy" (a phrase originating from Yangzi). The second sentence clarifies that the practice is direct pointing to the gate of contemplation, rather than regarding the treasures of others; hence it is called "cultivation."
The four lines following "Treating the moon" refute attachment; some say the finger represents the teaching that expresses [the truth], while the moon and the shore represent the principle expressed.

I now fear this initial metaphor uses the finger to represent the commentary and the moon to represent the sutra—just as one understands the sutra through the commentary, or sees the moon by means of the finger.
The subsequent metaphor uses the boat to represent contemplative practice and the shore to represent rebirth, which is attained through such practice.
Rebirth is like crossing to the other shore by means of a boat. Thus, one should not overvalue these two metaphors. The *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra* (*Yuánjué jīng*) states:
"The teachings of the sūtras are like a finger pointing at the moon; one must understand that what the finger points to is ultimately not the moon.

The *Diamond Sūtra* states: "Know that my preaching of the Dharma is like the metaphor of a raft. Even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not the Dharma" (and so forth). This clearly elucidates [the point].
Regarding the first four lines of the mind’s intent, which follow and uphold the two sages to extend their grace to future generations:
Vaidehī, through her great skillful means, initiated the Pure Land teaching not for herself alone, but to look down compassionately upon the末世 (final age). As the Sūtra says:

"If, after the Buddha's parinirvāṇa, all sentient beings are oppressed by the five sufferings of turbid, evil, and unwholesome conditions, how shall they be able to see Amitābha Buddha and the world of Ultimate Bliss?"
Furthermore, it is said: "How should future sentient beings contemplate Amitāyus Buddha and the two Bodhisattvas?

Now, this commentary is applied specifically to future audiences, much like the earnest entreaty of Vaidehī; thus, it is said that [the author] does not fail to honor the legacy of the final instructions.
When the Tathāgata first descended into the dark palace (the womb) and preached the Dharma, the listeners were few; he repeatedly instructed Ānanda with this underlying intent:
The *Gṛdhrakūṭa-sūtra* (Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa) states again: "Ānanda, you should receive and uphold this, and extensively proclaim the Buddha’s words for the sake of the great multitude.

It further says: "You should uphold the Buddha’s words and, for the sake of all the great assemblies of future ages who wish to be liberated from suffering, preach this 'Contemplation of the Earth Dharma' and so forth.
This present commentary respectfully upholds the intent of that final entrustment; as it is no different from the re-proclamation by Ānanda [at Vaiśālī], it is thus stated.

"May I not forget" means "I dare not forget. The following two phrases precisely express my original intention. "Supreme Vehicle" (shàngchéng) refers to this present sutra, for it is not partial or small;
thus, it is said to "surpass all others. This is merely a concluding phrase for what precedes.

In the opening section of this text, the first phrase indicates that which is about to be undertaken. The following four phrases are divided into two major sections to clarify both the general and specific meanings.

If one were to explain only the specific passages, the great significance would not be revealed; if one were to discuss only the general meaning, one would be confused regarding its origin and conclusion.
If these were explained in a muddled fashion, there would be no clear point of reference for either. Therefore, it is necessary to first extract the great significance contained within the sutra.
In the section preceding the individual texts, the general introduction is presented first; thus, the purport of the entire scripture becomes as clear as looking at one's own palm.

Subsequently, the individual texts and their phrases are explained in sequence, so that they remain in latent harmony with the general meaning. Since the general and the specific mutually encompass one another and the beginning and end form a single thread, this constitutes the gateway to the meaning (*arthamukha*).
Therefore it is said: "If one does not enter this gateway, one cannot perceive its beauty and richness. Herein, for a moment...
I have repeatedly questioned you to resolve the doubts of the age. Since ancient times, the propagation of the teachings has each had its designated custodian;

since you, Lingzhi, specialize exclusively in the Vinaya section, how could you possibly compose a commentary on the *Sūtras*? Is this not like a ritual officiant overstepping the sacrificial vessels to act as a cook? Answer:
Observing your questions, do they not reveal a mind as tangled as wild grass and a narrow, biased vision? Furthermore, the holy teachings of the Tripiṭaka are shared by the whole world.

Why should one differentiate between them? Thus, the Indian monks who came to this land and the high-ranking masters of this soil were some called "Tripitaka" (Masters of the Three Baskets) and others titled "Trisikṣā" (Masters of the Three Studies);
how could they be those who possess only a single wheel? Tiantai specifically propagated the Sūtras;

it is not that he did not discuss the Vinaya—for instance, his *Zhi guan chuyuan ji jie* (The Essentials for Cultivating Samatha-Vipaśyanā and Maintaining Pure Precepts) and his *Fan wang jie shu* (Commentary on the Brahma Net Sūtra Precepts) are evidence of this. Nanshan, however, exclusively...
Although Quan was not unacquainted with the sūtras and śāstras, he primarily adhered to the precepts;

he translated scriptures by imperial decree, composed prefaces for three sūtras, lectured on the *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, and compiled the *Fahua Yiyuan*. While each of these traditions has its own specific domain, one must not be a partisan in their study and understanding.
As for those such as Liu Qiu and Li Zhangzhe of antiquity, or the Duke of Jing and Zhang Tianjue of today—they were Confucians.
The scholar further understands Buddhist scriptures; how could there be a son of the Śākya who cannot master the sūtras? I asked Nanshan:

"If even within your own school you are still hindered by what you have not heard, how much less can you fully explain other sūtras and śāstras? Since the Patriarchs strictly observed the precepts, how can you willfully violate them?

He replied: "Riding on empty air and echoing sounds has been the practice for a long time. I shall now clarify it for you: this text is actually from the *Nanshan Jieben* (Nanshan’s Vinaya Precepts)."
In the commentary on the precept against great falsehood, because the *Prātimokṣa* speaks of the "Dharma of a Superior Person" (*uttaramanuṣyadharma*),

ancient masters have extensively cited sūtras and śāstras to interweave the characteristics of dhyāna with the essentials of the Vinaya school regarding observance and violation. Consequently, later students spend days in discussion without realizing that within the Vinaya,
the sūtras spoken therein are called "sūtras following the Vinaya," and within the sūtras, the Vinaya spoken therein is named "Vinaya following the Sūtra."

The Vinaya can only be briefly explained in terms of its names and characteristics; it should not be elaborated upon to the point of confusing the fundamental path. Therefore, did our Patriarch not leave behind these clear instructions?

Has he ever failed to permit the simultaneous mastery of both the Sūtras and the Śāstras? Have you not heard that our Patriarch established the *Yìyuàn* (Garden of Meanings) and lectured on the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*?

Regarding this Sūtra, which has circulated in the world since ancient times, there have been many schools of interpretation; among them, the Tiantai [commentaries]— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.]
The Commentary (*Shu*) flourished greatly in the southeast; all people treasure it more than gold or jade.

How much more so this [work], which was personally received at the Sacred Peak (*Ling-yue*), where one attained the wondrous realization of Great Awakening (*Da-su*) and obtained the revolving power of *dhāraṇī*, such that its joyful exposition is unobstructed.

If one were now to produce a separate new commentary, would it imply that Tiantai had something he did not yet understand? Answer: This is merely each person expressing their own aspirations. Generally, when virtuous men leave behind works for the world to establish...

In all his words and deeds, he prioritized praising the Buddha’s transformation and guiding sentient beings; how could this compare to the petty strife and pursuit of momentary victory found in the marketplace?
Regarding the common karma of past and present, there have been many who have offered their respective commentaries upon a single sutra.

For instance, while the *Fahua Wenju* (Words and Phrases of the Lotus Sutra) by Tiantai was already circulating in the world, the Dharma Master Cien appeared again during the Tang Dynasty to produce his own work.
Regarding the commentaries on the *Amitābha Sūtra*, following Tiantai, Huiyuan, Shandao, and Chengguan successively produced works.
Furthermore, Gushan and Zechuan, who both followed the Tiantai school, each composed their own sub-commentaries (*shuchao*) on the *Miaofa Lianhua Jing* (Lotus Sūtra).

This is because the purport of the teachings is profound and subtle, and individual intellectual capacities differ; the ocean of the *Prajñāpāramitā* can only be fathomed by a Buddha—Candrakīrti himself still considered it [inexhaustible].
The fact that Maitreya is not yet an omniscient one and must wait for the Way of the Dragon Flower to inquire further about the path is precisely this matter.
As for what is recorded here, it may be that the capacities and conditions are unequal or that knowledge and insight differ;

yet, in establishing karmic connections with beings and assisting the Buddha in spreading the transformation, the principle is perhaps appropriate—why must one seek out others to question? Whenever Tiantai explains a sutra, he invariably has a fixed rule.
The standard remains: first, one uses the five periods and eight teachings to distinguish and judge; next, one employs the five meanings and three divisions to explain.
Since the Tiantai school’s tradition takes time and teaching as its essentials, how could the new commentary not follow them? Why simply apply it directly to the sūtra? The answer is:
since you already hold me accountable based on the Tiantai system of time and teaching, why are you so one-sided? The Master of the Commentary once said: "From antiquity to the present, all..."

Whether refuting or establishing, suppressing or exalting, such is the universal rule for composition and the constant practice of scholarly discussion. Among the various treatises of the Western Heaven (India), the Great and Small Vehicles attack one another;

whether the proponents of Emptiness and Existence race in contention, or those of Nature and Characteristics act as fierce adversaries, their divergent attachments and fragmented views have continued unabated until the present day.
As for the transmission of the teachings here in this land (China), there are the traditions of Huayan Xianshou, Tiantai, and Ci'en.
Commentaries and exegeses circulated in competition, mutually refuting and supplanting one another;

this was much like the Confucian tradition, where the *Spring and Autumn Annals* of the Lu history opened into five transmissions, the *Gao Feng* and *Ya* odes were divided into four poems, Mencius’ discourse excluded Yang Zhu and Mo Di, and Master Xunzi took no account of Laozi and Zhuangzi.
Furthermore, between Zheng Xuan and Wang Su, teacher and disciple engaged in contradictory discourse, while Liu Xiang and Liu Xin, father and son, held opposing views.
Regarding the debate over differences and similarities, as for the Chan school itself: since the arrival of Bodhidharma from the West, the robe and bowl were transmitted in succession;

yet from the time of the Fifth Patriarch downward, the schools split into the Southern and Northern lines, and the five houses branched out. How could one insist on judging these as right or wrong and thereby incite disputes?
(That text continues: It is just like before the Tiantai school, when the "Three Schools of the South" and the "Seven Schools of the North" each established their own gateways, while the Tiantai...

Furthermore, since the later divisions have established many more schools and propagated their teachings extensively, how can you suppress them and compel them to abandon what they have studied to follow your own learning?
Moreover, Tiantai’s transformation and practice spread across over sixty prefectures; I do not know who else they would have followed for instruction outside of this.

Generally speaking, the establishments of all these various schools do not fail to prioritize adapting to the capacities of sentient beings; thus, [your claim] that one is right and the others wrong is not a comprehensive argument.
Question: The Holy Master of Tiantai stood at the stage of the Five Ranks; he penetrated the characteristics of all dharmas and entered into profound resonance with the Buddha-mind.

In his exegesis of the sutras, his eloquence flowed like a cascading river, spontaneously and naturally in accord with the *Sūtras*. How could I, a novice of the new commentaries, dare to arbitrarily challenge or reject him?
To feign eccentricity and deviate from common sense, leading ignorant later students to oppose the scriptures and contradict the sages—whose fault is this?
Answer: Observe the new commentary (*shu*); it never once uses a single word to criticize Tiantai.

Regarding the discussions on the principles of teaching and contemplation (*jiao-guan*), phenomena and principle (*li-shi*), there are over ten such instances where Tiantai alone is taken as the standard.

As for other minor details, some are adopted and others rejected, each according to its own justification; these do not originate from personal whims, but are formed by fully gathering the strengths of various masters.
Regarding the new interpretations introduced within this school’s perspective, they likely arise because the Buddha’s intent is manifold and his teachings extend beyond specific treatises;

thus, it is as Nāgārjuna did when he commented on the sūtras by preserving various interpretations. It would be fortunate to adopt what is excellent in principle rather than what is excellent in sentiment.
As for the new commentary, since it lacks a temporal or doctrinal classification of the sūtra, it instead relies solely on the four gates of general and specific analysis.
In response to the question of whether this exposition is merely a personal opinion or is based on an established tradition, I answer:

because my studies were not modeled after Dao’an and my interpretations do not easily encounter difficulties, the four gates listed at the beginning of the *Jieshu* and *Yejiexingshu* composed by Nanshan (Duan Ji) are not without their doctrinal judgments.

For instance, within the "Gate of Subsuming the Teachings" (*shejiaomen*) of the *Jieshu*, he extensively cites the various masters’ systems of establishment—whether based on the three wheels, the transformative practices, or the prohibitions.

Regarding the classification of the teachings—whether by transformation or by precept, or even as extensively expounded in the sūtras and śāstras—their quantity is immense, as stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* regarding the two characters "half" (*ardha*) and "full" (*pūrṇa*), which encompass both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna.
As for the textual categories of the Tripiṭaka, some divide them into Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna, each establishing four collections (*catuḥ-piṭaka*).
In Mahāyāna treatises, however, only two collections are established, as these exhaustively encompass the teachings for both Bodhisattvas and Śrāvakas.

Regarding the new commentary, which follows the rules and principles of the Nanshan tradition, how could I dare to establish my own views? Being of shallow insight and limited learning, I fear that to hastily give rise to criticisms would be improper; I do not yet know if such a course is permissible. Question:

Beyond merely praising and describing the fundamental school, what is the intention behind this new commentary’s focus on the Pure Land and its specialized interpretation of this sutra? Answer: This has already been clarified above; furthermore, I shall express it by means of two points. First, the Master [Daoxuan] was deeply devoted to the Pure Land and had long cultivated the practice of reciting the Buddha’s name. Second, he was concerned that later generations might fail to understand the profound meaning of this sutra. Therefore, he composed this work to clarify its essential points and to provide a basis for future practitioners. This is the reason why he focused exclusively on this sutra. As for the second point, he feared that those who study the teachings of the Tathāgata might be confused regarding the true intent of the Pure Land. Thus, he specifically composed this commentary to resolve their doubts. These two points constitute the underlying purpose. Furthermore, he intended to demonstrate that the Pure Land path is the most accessible and direct way to attain birth in the West, thereby encouraging all sentient beings to cultivate it with diligence. This is the ultimate intent behind his composition. It is not that he disregarded other teachings; rather, he prioritized this particular method because he perceived its supreme efficacy for the salvation of beings.

This is the reason for his exclusive focus. Finally, he wished to show that the various practices of the Mahayana ultimately converge in the Pure Land. By clarifying this principle, he sought to lead practitioners toward the single path of universal deliverance. This is the final and most profound intention of his work. One should not view this as a narrow-minded preference, but rather as a manifestation of the Great Compassionate One’s skillful means. To criticize him for this would be to misunderstand the profound depth of his wisdom. Thus, we should respectfully accept and uphold this teaching, never again harboring doubts or giving rise to slander. This is the definitive conclusion.

First, although our own school’s Vinaya tradition primarily elucidates the observance and violation of precepts— and while Master Nanshan profoundly accords with the teachings of the *Awakening of Faith* to establish the Perfect School (*Yuanzong*),
extensively discussing nature, characteristics, consciousness-only, and the three contemplations— I fear that later students who fail to grasp the underlying intent may cling to names and forms,
causing their minds to have no place of rest; therefore, I have specifically expounded the single gate of the Pure Land as the ultimate destination.
Therefore it is said: "While alive, propagate the *vinaya*; at death, return to the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). Thus one's essential task is completed.
Second, this single dharma of the Pure Land is vastly different from other paths; yet by merely forming a vow and seeking [rebirth], one attains transcendence.

Alas, how many masters seek the Way in what is distant when it lies near, and seek the matter in what is difficult when it is easy! The commentaries and exegeses they have composed to explain and clarify [the teachings] inevitably become muddled.
The teachings of a single lifetime do not distinguish between the pure and the mixed; each venerates its own school’s tradition while alternately rejecting or establishing others.

Their textual meanings are vast and comprehensive, and their underlying purports are profound and subtle. Unless one has accumulated learning, penetrated the mysteries, and exhausted the investigation of the obscure and the rational, it is ultimately difficult to enter them—how much more so when impermanence is swift and the timing of birth and death is uncertain?
Thus, if one wishes to practice with urgency, hesitation leaves one at a loss for what to do. For this reason:
In composing this work, I have endeavored to maintain simplicity and avoid prolixity.

By clarifying the two lands and pointing directly to the shortcut of rebirth there, I hope that those of both sharp and dull faculties in the末代 (final age) may find it plain and clear upon opening the scroll and encountering the text;

they may then put it into practice immediately without needing to search extensively through sutras and treatises or traverse the various gates of the teachings—a feat indeed difficult to achieve in a thousand years.
Since this transformation occurred so suddenly, I urge my fellow practitioners to pay close attention to this. First, regarding the "Gate of Meaning" (Yimén) listed herein:
our Buddha descended as a spirit and established teachings according to the capacities of beings; one must seek the fundamental intent, and thus there is the first [gate].

Second, although the intent of the teachings is clear, people do not know how to choose between the Great and Small Vehicles or the pure and mixed doctrines, and thus there is the second [gate]. Since the Great and Small [Vehicles] have already...
First, there are three [sections] because if one does not understand the judgment (*viniscaya*), there is no basis for establishing the practices (*caryā*) that are explained.

Second, there are four [sections] because if the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are confused, human delusions will diverge along many paths; thus, they must be clearly distinguished. These four topical divisions (*catuḥ-prakaraṇa*) have textual aims that require one another in sequence, and the great outline of this entire work does not exceed them.
One should beforehand master these thoroughly so as not to be confused when encountering the actual text.

In the introductory section of the *Tongmingjiaoxing xu* (Preface to the Rise of the Universal Illumination Teaching) explaining the Buddha’s intent, the first sentence designates the secular convention of taking thirty years as a "generation" (*dai*);

here, however, it refers generally to an entire cycle of transformation. Below this, the text correctly demonstrates that "Great Enlightenment" (*Dajue*) specifically refers to Śākyamuni; the Sanskrit term *Buddha* is translated here as "The Awakened One.
Because his realization is ultimate and perfect, he is called "Great"; because there is nothing in the mundane or supramundane worlds that surpasses him, he is so named.
Regarding the singular claim that the Honored One "manifests traces from the origin," Master Zao said:

"Without the origin, there would be no way to manifest the traces; without the traces, there would be no way to reveal the origin. Although the origin and the traces differ, they are fundamentally one in their inconceivability. The meanings of origin and trace vary according to distance:
from a remote perspective, one takes the very first instance of Śākyamuni’s attainment of enlightenment as the origin; thus, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states:
In truth, since I attained Buddhahood, it has been immeasurable, boundless hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of nayutas of kalpas.
For example, suppose there were five hundred thousand million billion nayutas of asankhyeyas of trichiliocosms, and someone were to grind them into fine dust;
if one were to pass that many lands to the east and drop a single grain of dust, and continue to drop one grain of dust for each land passed—

"Since my attaining Buddhahood has already passed through kalpas exceeding these, [the Buddha] here points to Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū as the 'original' and to today’s site of Śākyamuni’s enlightenment as the 'proximate.
This is the original within the traces; yet if one looks toward the ultimate original, it still belongs to the category of traces.
While various texts may take the Dharmakāya as the original and the Nirmāṇakāya as the trace, since we are not currently discussing his long-term lifespan,"

For the time being, "measure" (*pramāṇa*) refers to Vairocana of the Quiescent Site as the "root" and Śākyamuni as the "trace. The designations of "root" and "trace" do not apply to a single location;
this has been extensively discussed by Tiantai and cannot be set forth in full here. To clarify the original intent for what follows:
the Buddha’s wisdom intends to provide those below with the mind capable of salvation, thereby revealing the Dharma through which they may awaken and enter so as to be able to cross over.

Seeing that which is to be done refers to the sentient beings who are the objects to be delivered. However, regarding the "opening, showing, awakening, and entering" (*kaishijōnyū*) in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, interpretations by ancient masters have differed.
The ancients attributed "opening and showing" to the Buddha’s response and "awakening and entering" to the capacity of the disciples. Tiantai refuted this, stating:

"We do not adopt this interpretation for the sake of explaining the sūtra; rather, it is clear that all four phrases—'for the sake of causing sentient beings'—have both the words and the meaning centered entirely upon the sentient beings."

The previous discussion regarding the conditions for the audience was not concerned with the subject of transformation; thus, [the author] cited the *Lotus Sūtra* treatise as evidence and added further explanatory commentary.
As the text is extensive, it is not recorded here. However, the meaning of the current passage must necessarily be divided into two parts.

Why? Because since the text states, "for the purpose of opening and showing to sentient beings," we know that the one who can open and show is the Buddha, while the act of causing them to awaken and enter belongs to the teaching itself.

The meaning of the text is clear and manifest; there is no need for stubborn adherence. If this were so, would it not contradict not only Tiantai’s interpretation but also the intent of the sutra itself?

Answer: Tiantai’s primary purpose was to explain the sutra text. Since the sutra first mentions "sentient beings" and subsequently mentions "opening and revealing," all four phrases must be understood in relation to the capacity of the audience (*jī*).
The present commentary does not do so; it first mentions "opening and revealing" and subsequently mentions "sentient beings."
The *Sheng* merely borrows from that text to briefly clarify the intent of the transformation; thus, it differs from Tiantai’s formal exegesis.

As for the passage in the Sūtra beginning with "Below," it cites evidence to illuminate the preceding text; since the established doctrine and its underlying intent are distinct, they are not contradictory.

"Opening" (*kāi*) means to develop and reveal; "indicating" (*shì*) means to point out—both belong to the Responsive Body (*nirmāṇakāya*). "Awakening" (*wù*) refers to understanding and realization; "entering" (*rù*) refers to verification.

"Entering [the world] belongs to the occasion" (The correct cause, though divided into two parts, does not address the difficulty raised; although the "Aiding Contemplation" follows the Tiantai school, it does not understand the present meaning). Regarding the following two sections, which correctly clarify the arising of the response according to the times and the manifestation for the benefit of all:
the text is derived from the *I Ching*, the Qian hexagram, where both the second and fifth lines state, "It is advantageous to see the Great Man.

This clarifies that when a ruler emerges from concealment and ascends to the throne, he must accord with the hearts of the times, and all things ought to behold him. Now, this is borrowed [for our purpose].
Those words clarify that the Tathāgata’s capacity has arisen and the conditions for beings have matured;

thus, desiring to manifest his descent into the world to skillfully guide them, he—a great agent—spans from the initial attainment of enlightenment to the final entry into *nirvāṇa*, spreading the net of the Teaching to scoop up all capacities and cause them all to become Buddhas.
Therefore, it is called "Great" (as the term appears in the *Mencius*). The three passages cited below in the sutra provide sincere evidence for this.

The phrase "that which is enacted" (yǒu suǒ zuò) generally refers to the transformative teachings of a single lifetime, thereby verifying the aforementioned great purposeful action (*saṃskṛta*). The phrase "always" (*cháng*) below verifies the aforementioned original intent for transcending the world.

Since the Buddha’s intention has nothing else, it is said that he "always acts for one thing," which is precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). The "all-encompassing wisdom" (*sarvajñatā*) constitutes "knowledge," while the "Buddha-eye" (*buddhacakṣus*) constitutes "vision.
Sentient beings inherently possess this [wisdom and vision], yet they are deluded and do not realize it; it is only upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* that they directly [realize it].
It points out that the ordinary mind is itself the Buddha-mind, and that the physical eye is suddenly identical to the Buddha-eye;

thus, the original intent for transcending the world is finally fulfilled herein. This twofold manifestation of the Dharma-body consists of two parts: the first part contains three phrases which follow upon the preceding account of the arising of the teaching, the birth, and the parinirvāṇa.

By citing the beginning and the end, it encompasses the middle. The "teachings of sound" throughout the entire dispensation are collectively termed the Three Piṭakas; when the Tathāgata was in the world, they issued from his golden mouth.

Because the sound personally proclaimed by the Buddha constitutes the essence of the teaching, it is called "the teaching of sound. Although the traces of the teaching are mostly divided into the "half" and the "full," they are fully encompassed therein.

The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "The half-syllables are teachings of incomplete meaning; the full-syllables are teachings of complete meaning" (and so forth). Do not [interpret this] as merely following the previous intent of the Buddhas;

rather, it correctly clarifies the essence of the Dharma and exhaustively investigates the source of transformation. Therefore, it says: "It causes all 'existences' (*bhava*) to be collectively designated as the triple world (*tridhātu*)."

Ordinary people who have attained a general realization on the preliminary stages and awakened to their own minds realize that the fundamental mind-nature is luminous, quiescent, eternally abiding, and unchanging;
yet, due to delusive thoughts, they do not recognize this themselves. Now, wishing to return to the source, they rely upon the teachings to initiate cultivation;
as the nature is revealed and emotional attachments vanish, this is not obtained from without—hence it is called "self-awakening. The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* says: "To know all phenomena is..."
The wisdom-body is accomplished through the nature of one's own mind and is not realized through another. The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "The deluded mind ceases of its own accord;
this cessation is itself Bodhi. This supreme, pure, and luminous mind is not obtained from others. Since it is so with my own mind, it is likewise for all Buddhas and sentient beings.
Therefore, the text fully elucidates the three dharmas for self-awakening to one's own mind and mental phenomena—the Buddha-dharma of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
Furthermore, the Dharma-realm is the Dharma of all sentient beings and living creatures. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states: "As it is with the mind, so it is with the Buddha;

as it is with the Buddha, so it is with sentient beings. Mind, Buddha, and sentient beings—these three are without distinction in essence. Following this, the text further explains this mind by means of the Three Virtues (*tri-guṇa*).
The first two lines clarify the magnitude of its essence, which is like the great void, entirely free from obstruction: this is the virtue of *prajñā*.
The first four phrases clarify that the body-virtue (*kāya-guṇa*) is fully endowed with the virtue of liberation (*vimukti-guṇa*), such that all phenomena are without exception complete therein.
The final two phrases clarify that the nature of the body is fundamentally free from defilement and lacks any spatial location; this is the Dharma-body virtue (*dharmakāya-guṇa*).
These three are identical to the one, and the one is identical to the three; they are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither simultaneous nor distinct, being naturally and inherently possessed.
The preceding section explained the mind that has been perfected through provisional cultivation. Now, the ten lines below provide a general clarification of its pervasive manifestation:

although the single mind possesses the three virtues, there is a fear that one might mistake all phenomena for existing far removed from the mind. Therefore, following the intent of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, this is further demonstrated.

A bubble on the water and a fragment of cloud serve as metaphors for those various phenomena; the great ocean and the vast clarity of the sky serve as metaphors for one’s own mind. Second, the text cites a passage to demonstrate this.
In the first section of the middle [division], the initial citation from the root sūtra identifies "this mind" as the practitioner’s own mind of mindfulness of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*).

Because one practices according to the teaching and attains the fruit through this cause, it is said that "this mind makes the Buddha. Although Buddhahood is accomplished through provisional cultivation, it is not obtained from without;
therefore, it is said that "this mind is the Buddha. This refers to one of the ten titles of the Perfectly All-Knowing One (*samyaksambuddha*), which is vast horizontally and deep vertically.
This is illustrated by the profound analogy of the ocean. Because the ultimate fruit-virtues and causal mind are fundamentally inherent, it is said that they "arise from the mind and thoughts.
This immediately concludes and reveals that they are none other than the three virtues: Bodhi (wisdom), Prajñā (insight), and Nirvāṇa (liberation)—that is, the Pure Dharmakāya.
These words originate from the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, which states: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have been unable to achieve [this]."
Supreme Bodhi is entirely due to not knowing two kinds of roots: first, the root of beginningless birth and death, which is your present state of taking the攀緣心 (攀緣心;
*pān-yuán-xīn*, the mind that clings to objects) as its own nature;
second, the originally pure essence of beginningless Bodhi and Nirvana, which is your present *shí-jīng* (識精, consciousness-essence), the original luminosity capable of giving rise to all conditions.

Regarding that which was omitted by the *Yuan*: "The three are not fixed as three; the three are in fact one. It further explains: "This is precisely the single, true realm (*ekārtha-dhātu*) of the Mahāyāna;

because it is entirely one's own mind, it is said to be 'not another dharma'. Next, citing the *Zhancha shan'e baoying jing* (Sūtra on Examining the Retribution of Good and Evil), the full title of which is in two fascicles:
this citation is from the lower fascicle, from the beginning up to the section on "calculation" (*jì*).
All that belongs to "I" (the self) is fundamentally based on the scriptural text; that text is very extensive, and the final two lines were supplemented by the commentators.

The first section clarifies that the true mind is unchanging; although the three virtues (*triguṇa*) were pointed out therein as being identical to the single reality (*ekasatya*), this was done from the perspective of meaning.

Now, I shall again cite the text to manifest and demonstrate this clearly, desiring thereby to introduce the subsequent section on how delusion arises from the truth, which serves as the framework for establishing the teachings.
It is because of this fundamental principle that this section arises. The first phrase establishes the ultimate non-duality, termed "One";
its distance from delusion and falsehood is termed "Real. Because all Buddhas and sentient beings dwell within it, it is called the "Realm.
The second phrase points back to one's own mind to verify the preceding meaning. Since the previous section unified the three virtues and returned them to the single reality, this section further...

The one reality is divided into three virtues to manifest the identity of the three; their perfect interpenetration—neither identical nor separate—reveals that the essence of the Dharma is inconceivable.
From this point downward, it is shown that the three virtues are fundamentally unborn from the beginning and are now unextinguished.
Therefore, non-arising and non-extinction is the virtue of the Dharmakāya; the radiance of great wisdom is free from all defilements of delusion, and is thus the self-nature.
Purity is the virtue of *prajñā*; responding to conditions and manifesting according to stimuli, it is all-pervasive.
Therefore, its perfection throughout the ten directions is the virtue of *vimukti*. These three virtues are inherently complete and inseparable;

thus, they are called the "ultimate single characteristic. Next, to clarify how deluded thoughts follow conditions: the substance of the sentient being's mind is both quiescent and luminous, which is termed *dharmatā*. Once deluded, however—
This entire substance of the mind moves in darkness and transforms into the substance of ignorance (*avidyā*). Since its substance has completely turned, its function likewise undergoes a reversal;

the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*) are obscured, and the three paths (*tri-mārga*) consequently manifest. The first three phrases refer to the path of affliction (*kleśa-mārga*); the following three phrases beginning with "delusion" (*mṛṣā*) refer to the path of karma (*karma-mārga*);

and the final two phrases beginning with "extinction" (*nirvāṇa*) refer to the path of suffering (*duḥkha-mārga*). The *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "Because they do not penetrate the single Dharma-realm, the mind becomes non-concordant and suddenly..."
However, the arising of thought is called ignorance (*avidyā*); since there is no illumination of wisdom, the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of delusion and darkness arise.
As the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "It is like a worldly garment that originally has no fragrance; yet, because it is perfumed by someone with incense, it comes to possess a scent.
This is also the case here: the pure dharma of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is fundamentally free from defilement, yet it is perfumed solely by ignorance."

Because of habitual practice, there is the characteristic of defilement; although the dharmas of defiled ignorance truly lack pure karma, because they are perfumed by True Suchness (tathatā), there is the function of purity.
One should know that perfuming pervades both the defiled and the pure:

when deluded, ignorance perfumes True Suchness, giving rise entirely to defiled functions; when awakened, True Suchness perfumes ignorance, giving rise entirely to pure functions. Now, in this case...
Furthermore, speaking in terms of delusion and defilement, "causes and conditions" refers to deluded thought as the cause and deluded objects as the condition.
As the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* states: "Relying on the cause" means the sense of non-enlightenment; "relying on the condition" means the sense of falsely creating objective realms.

Regarding "delusory manifestation," the *Samantabhadra-bodhisattva-sarvatathāgata-tattvasaṃgraha-vinirdeśa-śāstra* (Zhan-cha) says: "One should know that external appearances are like the various realms seen in a dream; they exist only..."

One should contemplate that what is conceived in the mind is not real and that there are no external objects; all objective realms are likewise thus, for they are all produced by the deluded thoughts seen in the dream-like consciousness of ignorance.
This is because the false mind and false objects, through the conjunction of causes and conditions, create various false karmas and undergo various false retributions.
As the three paths of existence mutually support one another in an unbreakable cycle, it is said that one is "sunk and drowned" in birth and death, and so forth.

The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "All sentient beings, from time immemorial, have experienced the continuous succession of birth and death because they do not know the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure luminosity;
by employing various false thoughts, and because these thoughts are not real, they undergo transmigration. It further states:
"Because sentient beings have abandoned this fundamental luminosity, although they act all day long, they remain unaware of it, and thus they enter into various [states of suffering] in vain."

The preceding section has generally clarified the fundamental intent of transcending the world. As for the various commentaries that confuse the text and obscure the meaning, I do not wish to point them out directly;
let the student see their merits and defects for themselves upon encountering them. Second, regarding the exposition of the teaching, the first section of the text is divided into three parts:

first, a general clarification of the sutra; second, citing evidence from below; and third, specifically indicating those who have attained prior awakening. Mencius records that Yi Yin said: "I, under Heaven..."
Those among the people who are first awakened intend to awaken these people through this Way; for if it were not I who awakened them, who else would?
Now, if one borrows those words to express their meaning, the intent is different (and so forth). This mind is precisely the aforementioned single, true realm, the wondrous mind of the three virtues.
Thus, when the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata perceives sentient beings on the stages of realization as being deluded and unawakened, he gives rise to great...
Out of compassion, he entered the burning house to deliver and liberate beings; therefore, it is said that he "pities those who have not yet awakened.
This refers to the skillful means of compassion and mercy used to deliver sentient beings. It refers to the preaching of various sūtras, which are the dharma-gates for delivering beings.

Since these various sūtras are general and diffuse, they are clarified through the *Avataṃsaka* and the Deer Park teachings, representing the sudden and gradual approaches. Thus, the Tathāgata first, at the site of enlightenment (Bodhimaṇḍa), addressed those with the capacity of the "high mountain" type.

It is said that the Perfect Teaching does not come gradually but speaks directly of the sudden; thus it is called "sudden revelation. For a certain class of limited-capacity practitioners, the sudden teaching provides no benefit;

therefore, without moving from the site of tranquility (the Bodhimanda), he traveled to the Deer Park to preach the Dharma of arising and ceasing to accommodate them—thus it is called "gradual induction.
Although the sudden and the gradual differ, both are speech according to the intentions of others; when one investigates the Buddha’s original intent, [it is found to be otherwise].
To cause [beings] to enter the true darkness, the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* is employed to support and establish this meaning; thus it says, "returning to the source," and so forth.

In the cited evidence, the first passage—concerning those of small wisdom and small teachings—is restricted to the gradual realization of the various gates above. The second passage—concerning the manifold aspects—must encompass both sudden and gradual realizations as being non-dual.
This is because, in the past, the Buddha-vehicle was kept secret and not discussed, following the intent of the *Lotus Sūtra*.

By making this statement, the Master [of the Commentary] internally reflects that because the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma varies according to the capacities of sentient beings, he distinguishes the holy teachings of his entire life into two lands (*dvīpa*) with differing approaches to entering the Path.
This serves as a preliminary foundation for the doctrinal classification (*panjiao*) to be presented in the subsequent text, as will be explained later;
thus, there is no need for further elaboration here. Although the preceding and succeeding sections are divided into two distinct parts, both are ultimately the Tathāgata.
Coming to transform others through skillful means, when one investigates their ultimate destination, there is nothing that does not serve to cause sentient beings to become Buddhas.

In the first part of this text, it clarifies that by relying on the teaching, one opens up understanding such that one’s own mind is directed toward the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*). Although phenomena are numerous, they do not transcend the ten realms of the mutual coexistence of the environment and its inhabitants, causes and effects;

these all reside within the single mind. Once the single mind is awakened, every phenomenon is entirely the mind, and mind, phenomena, and the Dharma are of one suchness. Therefore, it is said: "Penetratingly."

Next, the following clarifies the cultivation of causes and the realization of the fruit. The first phrase refers to the arousal of the Great Mind; the second phrase refers to the cultivation of the Great Practice;

the final two phrases refer to the attainment of the Great Fruit. This includes the aforementioned "penetrating understanding," which constitutes the opening of Great Wisdom. The former three belong to the cause, while the latter one belongs to the fruit. Cause and fruit are simultaneous, and the two minds are not distinct.
Below this, the third section clarifies the arising of function after the realization of the fruit. The initial four phrases [do not...]
Abandoning the two extremes and dwelling solely in the Middle Way, one encompasses both *paricchinna-vipariṇāma* (segmented) and *pariṇāma* (transformative) birth-and-death.

To shatter the delusions of affliction and emerge from the suffering of saṃsāra, the merit lies in wisdom; to encompass both *sopadhiśeṣa* (with remainder) and *nirupadhiśeṣa* (without remainder) nirvāṇa while teaching and transforming sentient beings—losing oneself to benefit others—the merit lies in compassion.
Throughout the lower stages, this correctly demonstrates the Great Function: namely, that when the realm of sentient beings is exhausted...
My birth-karma is exhausted and the afflictions of sentient beings are exhausted; thus, this King of Vows of mine has no end.
In the cited scriptural passages, the two sutras mentioned merely serve to prove the aforementioned meaning that [the Buddha] manifests birth and proclaims extinction, yet remains inexhaustible.

Regarding the first passage from the *Avataṃsaka*, in terms of his own practice (*sva-caryā*) there is none, but in terms of transforming others (*parārtha*) there is; hence the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* says: "I do not truly enter parinirvāṇa now," and so forth.

He then proclaimed: "I shall enter parinirvāṇa. Why is this? Because if those of meager merit were to see the Tathāgata as always present and never passing away, they would give rise to arrogance, self-indulgence, and a mind of indolence;
they would not conceive the thought that such a being is difficult to encounter, nor would they develop a heart of reverence.
For this reason, the Tathāgata speaks thus through skillful means. Now, these two phrases from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* appear difficult to distinguish; I fear...

The first phrase speaks in terms of the past, stating that there has never been heard of a Buddha entering *nirvāṇa*; the second phrase discusses the present, asserting that there is likewise no Buddha currently about to enter *nirvāṇa*.
That the scriptural passages are arranged in this reciprocal manner is certainly not without purpose. The three concluding points indicate the central meaning;

therein, the two characters "this is called" (*shì wèi*) universally point to the fundamental intent behind the arising of the teachings throughout the entire dispensation. As for the "great cause and condition" (*dàshì yīnyuán*), it refers to the supreme [teaching] within the sutra.
There is a one-character *Tiantai* commentary which states: "One" refers to the One True Reality (*ekasatyatā*). "Great" means that its nature is vast and expansive.

It is the ritual procedure for the appearance of all Buddhas in the world; therefore, it is called a "phenomenon" (*vastu*). When sentient beings have a resonance with the Buddha, this constitutes the cause (*hetu*);

the Buddha then responds to that resonance, which constitutes the condition (*pratyaya*). This is the fundamental intent of appearing in the world. Since the Way is the same for every Buddha, it is so stated.
Since all these ultimately converge upon this point, it is said that "it is here.

Within the first section of the present sutra, there are two subsections: the first clarifies the arising of the capacity [of the audience] and their request for the Dharma; the second clarifies the response to that capacity through the manifestation of the teaching.

Within the first of these, the initial phrase introduces the subject, while the subsequent portion specifically demonstrates the "trigger" (jī). The "trigger" refers to the bow-snap; it signifies the capacity [of the seeker].
The meaning of "being able to be inspired" serves as a metaphor for Vaidehī seizing the opportune moment to present her request; thus it is said that the "capacity has been aroused.

Because King Ajātaśatru committed treason and felt no fear or restraint, it is said he acted "publicly. One should know that all of this is a manifestation of great skillful means (*mahopāya-kauśalya*).

He observed that a certain class of sentient beings in the末代 (final age) possessed the karmic seeds for the Pure Land, yet these were appropriately kept hidden within their hearts and could not be spontaneously aroused. Therefore, he specifically provided a vigorous proclamation to strike them awake.
To this day, all people receive its benefits. The meaning of these two passages is fully explained in the subsequent commentary.
Within the separate listing of ten sections, each first establishes a thesis and subsequently cites scriptural evidence. Observe that the sequential arrangement of these ten points is not accidental;
the first three correspond to the three obstacles (*trividha-āvaraṇa*). Since sentient beings have been wandering through the three paths since beginningless time, they must now seek liberation.

First, as an antidote to the desire to destroy [the path], one must necessarily cultivate the two adornments (*dvaya-saṃbhāra*). Throughout kalpas of practice, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas have never transcended merit and wisdom;
therefore, the fourth [perfection] is the contributory cause (*upaniṣad-hetu*) of merit, and the fifth is the revealing cause (*vijñapti-hetu*) of wisdom.
Because of a lack of wisdom, one follows what is deviant and turns away from what is correct; now, wishing to return to the correct and overturn the deviant, wisdom is indispensable. (2)

Since the three trainings have already been fully prepared, one should accordingly observe them: thus, the sixth is the training in ethical discipline (*śīla*) which is pure through the removal of defilements;

the seventh is the training in concentration (*samādhi*) which causes the mind to abide in meditative absorption; and the eighth is the training in wisdom (*prajñā*) consisting of the Buddha-remembrance samādhi (*buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*). The first eight belong to the cause, while the latter two belong to the fruit.

The ninth is the manifestation of the body and the vision of the Buddha, wherein contemplation is perfected and principle is revealed; the tenth is the swift attainment of Buddhahood as the result of these causes.
