from the light, transformations manifest—all of these are the inconceivable functions of the Bodhisattva. Fifth, contemplating the arms, there are likewise three marks:
the arms are the color of red lotuses; from the colors, light is emitted; the light transforms into necklaces that encircle the Bodhisattva’s arms, further manifesting wonders.
Regarding the six marks, the hands are also observed in three ways; "the tips of the fingers" means that the tips are straight and upright.
Within the patterns, colors, and lights, there are likewise three layers each, totaling eighty-four thousand distinct and general variations.

As for the function of raising the middle hand to receive sentient beings, the *Mahākaruṇā-sūtra* states that the hands possess the power of uplifting and rescuing, while the eyes possess the function of illuminating, thereby representing the supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) of the Bodhisattva.
Wisdom is the spontaneous resonance [of these qualities]. Seventh, regarding the two signs of lifting and lowering the feet:
as for the "spoked wheel," the spokes are the wooden rims surrounding the hub; as the scripture says, "thirty spokes converge upon a single hub.

Eighth and ninth, the fleshy protuberance on the crown (*uṣṇīṣa*) is the mark (*lakṣaṇa*), while the invisible crown of the head is the excellence (*anuvyañjana*). Although a Bodhisattva possesses these, they do not yet equal [those of a Buddha].
Because the Buddha’s cause and fruit differ, the two contemplations of the knots rely on the scriptural passage concerning the *rūpakāya* (form-body);

therefore, they are judged to belong to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response-body), as previously demonstrated. Third, the exhortation to practice: the first section regarding the various marks refers to the preceding nine sections.

Within the "Manifesting Merit" [section], the two phrases "not encountering various calamities" and "purifying karmic obstacles" both manifest the difficulties. In the "Citing Analogies" [section], "obtaining merit" is like...
In the "Universal Gate" chapter (*Samantamukha-parivarta*), among the seven calamities and two petitions, there is none that does not involve invoking the name to receive a response.

Within the teachings on contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), since the physical marks and features of a Bodhisattva are numerous, a beginner is unable to contemplate them all at once; thus, the teaching proceeds by stages. The *uṣṇīṣa* (crown-protrusion) is the most honored feature of the entire body, so one begins with it.

From this, one proceeds to the remaining features, such as the celestial crown, the transformed Buddhas, and even down to the wheel-mark on the soles of the feet. Each [is to be contemplated in turn].
Because they have attained their respective places, they are said to follow a sequence.

Regarding the eleven subsequent explanations, the first section on the dimensions of the bodies can be understood by analogy with what preceded. In the second section on the characteristics of the light, regarding the first item—the light of Avalokiteśvara—it is stated to extend for hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*.
As for why the quantities differ, it may be because there are distinctions in the manifestations of the Bodhisattvas' transformations.

Alternatively, the narrator may provisionally distinguish these categories below, with all subsequent instances to be understood by analogy. "Illumination" refers to the function of light, which is doubled;

"the radiance of the body" refers to its extent throughout the ten directions, while "purple-gold" refers to its color. Next, regarding those who have the conditions: "conditions" refers to the seeds of past merit—whom does one not possess them?
It is simply that they differ in being raw or matured. This is designated as the first cause among the initial [causes], wherein light is seen from a single pore.

The light of the Buddhas differs in its causes and conditions, yet is identical in its internal realization. The Sūtra says it is "pure and wondrous": it is pure because the afflictions and defilements have been exhausted;

it is wondrous because the fundamental nature and virtues are inherently complete. Regarding the two [aspects] of "extracting" and "bestowing," it extracts the suffering of the two deaths and bestows the bliss of the three virtues.
The Ten Powers will be explained in detail later. The former name belongs to wisdom (*jñāna*), while the latter name belongs to compassion (*karuṇā*); thus, it is compassion within wisdom.

Compassion and wisdom, though established as two distinct entities in name, are in reality one and the same. This can be seen from the textual analysis of the *Sūtra on the Three Crowns and Four Uṣṇīṣas*.
As for why the uṣṇīṣa contains a jeweled flask, it symbolizes the Bodhisattva’s internal realization of the three virtues:
the jeweled flask represents the virtue of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); the radiance represents the virtue of Prajñā; and the Buddha-activities represent the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*).
Regarding the five remaining characteristics, either the compilers or the translators have merely presented those that differ while omitting those that are identical to avoid redundancy;
thus, as indicated in the preceding commentary, they briefly show the face, arms, and hands, hence the word "etcetera. Next, regarding the aspect of activity (*ākāra*):

if one wishes to express it in terms of phenomena, "activity" refers to the wisdom of the Bodhisattva who is able to contemplate, while "worlds" refers to the objects of contemplation—ten [directions].

Because the sentient beings within the realms do not depart from the essence of a single thought-moment of the Bodhisattva, and are thus able to destroy delusions and manifest principle, it is said that "all things tremble.
That which is called "the place where the earth shakes" refers precisely to the objective realm illuminated by the Bodhisattva’s contemplative wisdom;
since one can destroy delusions, one must necessarily give rise to practice. Therefore, the "five hundred billion precious flowers" are a metaphor for the true causes of the five stages.
Furthermore, because one cultivates merit and wisdom within the five stages, it is called "adornment" (*vyūha*); because cause and effect are non-dual, it is called "lofty and manifest.

The Land of Ultimate Bliss (*Sukhāvatī*) is precisely the realm of the true reality (*dharmatā*) that is realized. Among the three aspects of sitting, some wish to represent the Dharma by performing [the ritual] as before;
during the preaching of the Dharma, because of the previous movement, the emanated bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) are gathered together according to the sutra.
"Countless as the dust of immeasurable lands" is a metaphor for the vast number of intermediate lands; the *Sūtra Commentary* states that this "encompasses all Buddha-fields.

(The statement in the *Zhengyin* that "the body is not one" is an error. "Filling and obstructing" (*chìsè*) describes the state of being completely full; the *Sūtra Commentary* says it means "filling the void.
*Chì* is pronounced *chūzé*. The *Shuowén* says: "In tilling the crops, *chìchì* refers to advancing. This concludes the demonstration of the middle [state], which is the same as the previous two.

Contemplation corresponds to the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body). Within the section on manifesting benefits, since one is able to break through obstacles, one must certainly eliminate doubts; this can be seen in the subsequent section.
In the double conclusion, the Sūtra says, "the lands of all Buddhas," because by being born in one land, all lands are thereby accessible.

Is it not the removal of doubt that allows one to leave the womb and roam through Buddha-lands? From the crown of the head, which is the *uṣṇīṣa*, down to the feet, which are the *cakrāṅka* (wheel-marks).

Taking up the beginning and end while encompassing the middle, the Sūtra mentions both [the disciples] together because these two Great Beings were both attendants of the Buddha and shared a similar character;
the Commentary, following the text of the Sūtra, establishes and demonstrates the intent of the topical outline.

Regarding the twelve points for distinguishing the general from the specific within the preceding section: first, the initial example establishes the general based on what precedes; second, the two subsequent points correctly distinguish the general from the specific, which will be seen in the actual text.
First, as for the "specific," one contemplates each item individually, from the lotus seat up to Avalokiteśvara and Mahāsthāmaprāpta.

Following this, the "general" refers to contemplating these two contemplations together as a whole. This is stated in terms of a single person practicing the stages sequentially; the preceding contemplation [refers to the specific].

Although many sacred signs have been accomplished, there is a fear that they may be forgotten; therefore, following the three sages, one now contemplates them all blended as one, so that the particular does not depart from the general and the general does not depart from the particular.
When the general and the particular mutually encompass one another, the path of contemplation becomes thorough and skillful, and one enters, exits, and abides well—this is what is meant by this.
When contemplating universally, one visualizes within one's own body and, immediately following the previous stage, sees this matter at once.
The phrase "the preceding five contemplations" refers to those that initiate the subsequent [contemplation]. When the mind arises, one immediately forms a mental image (*saṃjñā*).

One imagines the body being born there, simultaneously seeing clearly all the primary and secondary marks (*lakṣaṇa*) of the Pure Land. When this mental image becomes fully matured, it constantly manifests before one;

even with eyes closed at the end of life, rebirth is certain. As the Sūtra says regarding "the sign of the eyes opening": because light comes to illuminate them, the eyes immediately open and become clear. (2)
Regarding the teaching on the convergence of all phenomena within the Universal Vision (*Samantadarśana*):

although the preaching of the Dharma pertains to the convergence or non-convergence of the *dharmakāya* (the primary) and the *rūpakāya* (the secondary), such matters are irrelevant to the practitioner's own practice.

One should know that while the preaching of the Dharma indeed concerns these two bodies, there is a fear that the practitioner’s contemplation may become biased or deviant, leading to the mistaken recognition of demonic realms (*māraviṣaya*). Therefore, it is instructed that one must not encounter [or be attached to] the teachings as they are heard.
If one accepts this with faith and verifies it through the standard of the noble ones (*ārya-pramāṇa*), then the true and the false can be distinguished.

This constitutes the primary retribution (*vipāka-phala*) of Amitāyus Buddha within the context of names and meanings, while the Land of Ultimate Bliss constitutes his secondary environment (*adhiṣṭhāna*).

Since it is revealed within the section on response and resonance that by practicing contemplative cultivation according to the teachings, when the merit is perfected and the conditions for the Pure Land are deepened, there is the certainty of rebirth; thus, one invokes the Three Sages, who respond by offering consolation.

Thirteenth, regarding the selection of the capacity (*yogya*), the Sūtra belongs to the *pariyāya-dharma* (teaching for transformation), as it follows or disregards the capacity according to circumstances; thus, it is not a fixed rule.

In the section on "First Contemplating the Small [Body]," the phrase "conforming to the capacity" means that because the people of this land are accustomed to seeing the sixteen-foot [body], they are first led to contemplate the small body of that land as a gradual means for contemplating the Great [Body].
The Sūtra’s mention of an "image" refers to the True Body (*dharmakāya*) of that land.
The physical image is not a false image. The *Dazhong jing* (Sutra of the Great Vehicle) later states that the dimensions of the body are boundless;

this serves as verification that the previously mentioned measure of sixty million *koṭis* of Ganges sands is a numerical manifestation rather than a literal limit, and thus there is no cause for doubt. Third, regarding the "analogy" (*jǔkuàng*) among the three [sections]:

as for "mental visualization" (*xiànxiàng*), it is as described in the aforementioned "Contemplation of the Image" (*xiàngguān*) and in the *Buddhānusmṛti-samādhi-sūtra*, which explains the methods of contemplating images and so forth, as well as the contemplation of reality (*zhēn*).

This refers to the small body of one zhang and six chi in the Pure Land, and the large body of eighty thousand [yojanas]. (The *Zhengyin* states that "the image" refers to what the practitioner visualizes;
this is incorrect. Regarding the four measurements being indeterminate, the sutra says: "That which is subtle and wondrous, difficult to fathom, is called 'spirit' (*shen*);

that which transforms without obstruction is called 'pervasion' (*tong*). "As one wishes" (*rúyì*) is one of the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). Although the Buddha has neither small nor large dimensions, his appearing as small or large is like a bright mirror.

When reflecting images, although there are ten thousand differences in the reflections, the substance of the mirror remains non-dual. Among the various characteristics of the five fingers, one should contemplate the body of the Buddha;
though their sizes differ, their golden hue is the same. As for the other fingers, they are as clearly explained in the preceding commentary.

Regarding the first section on contemplating the Bodhisattvas, the initial general point concerning sentient beings refers specifically to the assembly of disciples; this is because there was concern that the term "sentient beings" might be confused with those of the five turbidities, and thus it was specified here.

The following section specifically distinguishes [the classes] to clarify that there is no confusion between the middle and lower classes. Although those of the middle class who are *śrāvakas* and those of the lower class who are humans or devas are part of the retinue, they certainly do not intermingle with one another.

The subsequent section clarifies that there is confusion regarding the upper class; for the most part, these are those in their final birth before Buddhahood (*ekajātipratibaddha*), whose physical forms are indistinguishable from those of the two Great Beings (Bodhisattvas).
This present passage provides a specific distinction, and thus cites the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Small Version) as evidence. However, this is only the lower [part of the explanation].
Correcting the Text.
Regarding the reason why it is so stated in the fourteenth section, "The Contemplation of the Three Grades," which provides the formal judgment:

it is because all sixteen aspects of this sutra pertain to both the environment and the inhabitants (the *āśraya* and *sambhoga*) of that land, and both belong to the realm of contemplation for the practitioner. This has been the interpretation since antiquity.
The explanation of the different systems of establishment generally consists of two parts:
first, because the causal practices described in the sūtra text are mostly ritual acts (*vastu-karma*), the nine grades are categorized as belonging to the "scattered virtues" (*prādeśika-kuśala*);

second, based on the three classes of practitioners in the sūtra being entirely members of the Three Vehicles—including humans and devas—their respective stages and positions are distinguished and judged, [a view] shared by generations of contemplative practitioners in this land.

The delusion [concerning this] is addressed now by the Master of the Commentary, who, through innate wisdom and independent judgment, examines the text and summarizes the principles to resolve doubts and dispel ignorance.

Prior to the main text, he provides a concise analysis and discernment as clear as pointing at one's own palm. In the first three phrases of the main text, he generally indicates the nine grades, followed by a phrase that determines the object of contemplation.
The subsequent two phrases describe the causes of worldly delusion, which arises solely because the scriptural text provides a detailed exposition.
Because those three grades in that land represent the characteristics of practice cultivated during their causal stage, ancient masters identified them as people who wish to be born in this land.

Now, the following points clarify the intent of the sutra: the first three lines determine the present state, while the subsequent four lines correctly demonstrate what should be done. One should first raise the objection:
"Since these are the characteristics of those already born, why does the sutra describe them in this way? The explanation states: it is intended to lead future... [text ends]
Worldly practitioners recognize that there are nine grades [of rebirth] based on the original causal ground.

One should consider what kind of practice must be cultivated here to produce such a rebirth there, and what kind of fruit will be experienced therein, so as to cultivate the cause according to one's own capacity for the fruit.

Thus, although those already born [in the Pure Land] are divided into nine grades, when discussing those who wish to be born in this land, they are all ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), distinguished merely by the shallowness or depth of their meritorious conduct.
Regarding the depth of penetration and the speed of progress on the Path, it is like the system of the world where scholars are recommended for office:
though there may be thousands or tens of thousands, their talents and insights range from the clever to the clumsy with a difference as vast as heaven and earth;

yet none are not called "commoners" until they enter the examination hall to present their compositions and compete in skill, at which point the hierarchy of the first and second ranks is distinguished. The wise understand through parables; one should reflect deeply upon this analogy.
The citations from the ancient [texts] herein are precisely from the Tiantai commentaries (*shu*). They state that there are two meanings regarding the contemplation of those who attain rebirth:

first, to cause them to recognize the three grades of rebirth so that they may abandon the middle and lower grades and cultivate the superior grade; second, as cited in the commentary, to point out that [the superior grade] is not the middle.

Regarding the first point, if one relies on the three superior grades, then the middle and lower grades are excluded; furthermore, within the three superior grades, the causal practices are distinguished.
Upon consulting the sutra for collation, the text states: "As for those of the superior grade, they leave home, renounce desire, and become śramaṇas;
they give rise to the bodhicitta and single-mindedly and exclusively recollect Amitāyus Buddha, cultivating various meritorious virtues (and so forth).

Those of the middle grade give rise to the bodhicitta and single-mindedly recollect that Buddha, cultivating the roots of goodness, observing the fasts and precepts, erecting stupas and images, and providing food for the saṃgha."
Hanging silk banners at the gates, lighting lamps, scattering flowers, and burning incense (and so forth).

As for those of the lower grade who wish to be born in that land, even if they are unable to perform various meritorious deeds, they should resolve upon the unsurpassed mind of bodhi and focus their intent single-mindedly;

this constitutes ten recitations of the name of Amitāyus Buddha (and so forth). Comparing that with these three superior grades, it is difficult to say whether their minds and practices are the same or different.
This is a comparison and illustration among the lower grades (the remainder is as in the *Fuxin*). To clarify the Middle Way:
although those born within the worlds of the ten directions are numerous, when categorized by human type, they do not exceed three classes; when categorized by rank, they do not exceed nine grades.

Taking the entire assembly of disciples already born in that region as the object of contemplation for the present, the text now explicitly sets forth five dharmas, the first of which is the explicit listing of Bodhi.
The mind is precisely the Buddha-mind. The Buddha possesses no ordinary mind; he has only the mind of great compassion, which universally covers the Dharma-realm and benefits sentient beings;
therefore, it is called the "Great Mind. The ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) is precisely the Buddha-wisdom;

because it is developed in a single thought-moment and penetrates deeply to the source of the Dharma, it is called "Great Understanding. The practice of various deeds is precisely the Buddha’s conduct; thus it is stated in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*.
Furthermore, there is one practice called the Practice of the Tathāgata; because this single practice universally encompasses all practices, it is called the Great Practice.

Deeply believing in cause and effect is the faith of the Buddha. The cause of the Mahāyāna is the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena, and the fruit of the Mahāyāna is likewise the true reality of all phenomena.
Because one understands that cause and effect are not separate from true reality, it is called Great Faith, dedicated toward [enlightenment].
To aspire for rebirth is the vow of the Buddha; to realize that the Pure Land is one's own mind and that Amitābha is one's own nature is the Great Vow.
Because one seeks rebirth in the Pure Land of the Mind-only and aspires to behold the Amitābha of the Original Nature, it is called the Great Vow.

Through the opening of understanding by means of the mind, and through establishing practice based on that understanding, practice begins as the cause and culminates as the fruit. That which is cultivated throughout this process of cause and fruit is not even a hair’s breadth [different from the essence].
All wholesome roots are dedicated together with the vow to be reborn in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (*An-yang*). Among these five dharmas, it is impossible for even one to be missing;
as indicated by the presence or absence of terms in the following text, this will become clear below. Regarding the three grades, the first grade possesses all [five] without omission:
sincerity is the great mind; the profound mind is the great faith; the aspiration is the great vow; and the possession of precepts refers to the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*).

"Great Practice" (*mahācaryā*) refers to the recitation and study of the Mahāyāna; "Great Understanding" (*mahādhimukti*) refers to the four types of excellent understanding regarding the meaning and intent within the preceding section;

"Great Mind" (*mahācitta*) refers to the mind being unshaken by fear; "Great Faith" (*mahāśraddhā*) refers to deep faith in cause and effect; "Great Vow" (*mahāpraṇidhāna*) refers to the dedication and aspiration for enlightenment.
Although the text may omit the [explicit mention of] practice, the principle must not be absent. Furthermore, in the subsequent three sections, there is likewise great faith in cause and effect.

It also involves generating the unsurpassed mind and the great mind, as well as dedicating oneself through the aspiration for great vows. Regarding the two dharmas of understanding and practice, though the text is deficient here, their meaning is complete;
if one were to distinguish between their benefits and harms below, these five dharmas take the great mind as primary.

Understanding, practice, faith, and vows are inherently neither large nor small, yet they become "great" by virtue of the mind. Those who are born in the Pure Land do so without exception because of the great mind—how much more so those of the highest grade!
Having already attained rebirth in that land and established oneself in the rank of a Bodhisattva, how could one not resolve to attain the Great Mind?

Without faith, one would repudiate cause and effect; without aspiration, one would certainly not be drawn into rebirth. Thus, we know that if the fourth and fifth [preparations] are lacking, rebirth is impossible.

Below, the three grades are distinguished: the "Supreme Grade" refers to the Bodhisattva at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), which is the highest birth. The "Non-retrogressive" grade refers to...

From the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) onward, one is born into the upper and middle [realms]. The initial mind encompasses those who come from the ten directions to be born in the stage prior to abiding (*sthāna-pūrva*), which is the position of semblance (*sādṛśya-avasthā*);
this refers to birth in the upper and lower [realms].

Regarding birth in the upper [realms], the three minds are discussed in the first section; the Sūtra says, "If there are sentient beings," which indicates the seeking of the capacity (*yogyatā*). They vow to be born there.
The "Nation" (*rāṣṭra*) is the signifier; it indicates the three minds and clarifies the subsequent practice of conduct.

Regarding the first section of the commentary, the initial three phrases provide a general signification, while the following section provides a specific explanation of that signification. Within the signification, the essence of the three minds is designated as the "bodhicitta.
To be complete, one should say *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi-citta*. "Bodhi" is translated as "Path" (*mārga*). Since both the Chinese and Sanskrit terms are presented together, it is called "also."
This is called the mind of the unsurpassed path. Because it directly gives rise to the Buddha-mind and nothing can surpass it, it is termed "unsurpassed.
In the commentary, "sincerity" (zhicheng) refers to the nature (xing). Because practice accords with this nature, it is called "ultimate sincerity.

"Seeking the Buddha’s bodhi" means setting one's mind upon the ultimate fruit. "Remaining unshakable until Buddhahood" means there is no duality between the beginning and the end. "Profound mind" (shenxin) penetrates the Dharma.
The root source of the Mahāyāna is the perfect and sudden definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Hearing, contemplation, and cultivation are the three wisdoms within a single mind.
"Reaching Buddhahood without ceasing" refers to the infinite gateways of the Dharma. Regarding the citation of evidence below:

the *Prajñāpāramitā* (Perfection of Wisdom) is profound and vast without limit, metaphorically likened to the ocean. That the Buddha has reached its bottom refers to the bottom of that which has no bottom. This is the dedication and arousal [of the bodhicitta].

The phrase "the fundamental merit of the vow for rebirth is universally bestowed" refers to the pervasiveness of its scope; "reaching the inexhaustibility of the Buddhas" refers to the infinity of one's practice and vows.
Furthermore, these three minds are themselves the three causes of Buddha-nature (and so forth). While they may be spoken of as having a sequence, in principle there is no gradual progression;
whichever single mind is invoked, all three are fully present. This is what the Buddha praised as the "simultaneous arising of the three minds."

This is so. Regarding the three clusters (*triskandha*) among the three clusters, the name "three clusters" originates from the *Bodhisattvabhūmi*. Its meaning applies universally across various scriptures. The Mahāyāna precepts are equal in measure to space;
as one pursues objects and progressively receives them, there is no time when they are exhausted.

When categorized by type, they do not exceed three: abandoning evil, cultivating good, and saving sentient beings. The former two pertain to one's own practice, while the latter one pertains to transforming others. These are what the Bodhisattvas cultivate.

It is simply thus: these three clusters (triskandha) are also without distinction. One must certainly sever evil and cultivate goodness; yet, if one cultivates goodness, does one not thereby deliver sentient beings?

How much more so in the Mahāyāna’s three clusters! If there were indeed evil to be severed, goodness to be cultivated, or sentient beings to be delivered, such that phenomena existed apart from the mind, they would all belong to the partial and limited vehicles.
Only when each and every thing accords with its true nature (*dharmatā*) is it not otherwise than the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).

To fulfill the Perfect Teaching (as explained at length): among the three Buddhas, although there are many teachings concerning the three dharmas, the specific pairing of the three aggregates (*tri-skandha*) with the three Buddhas and the three minds is due to the fact that sentient beings in the five turbidities cannot escape [saṃsāra] without pure precepts;
yet these three minds are the very essence of the three Buddhas, for within this causal stage, one receives the three aggregates of precepts by means of these three minds.
In the future, one will certainly realize the fruit of the three Buddhas; how much more so now, when this sutra says, "This mind makes the Buddha; this mind is the Buddha.

When the minds of sentient beings are pure, the Buddha responds accordingly. To reveal that the causal mind inherently possesses the virtues of the fruition, and to cause practitioners to aspire to the fruit by cultivating the cause, this brief indication is given—how could it be in vain?
The *Ji yuan ji* states: "The essence of the consciousness of sentient beings..."
Originally pure and free from all defilements, it is through deluded conceptualization that it is transformed into afflictions (*kleśa*).

Furthermore, originally sovereign and fully endowed with skillful means, wisdom, majestic power, and virtuous function, it is through deluded conceptualization that it is transformed into fetters and karma.
Moreover, originally equal and devoid of distinctions such as self and other or love and hatred, it is through deluded conceptualization that it is transformed into...
Because one now wishes to return to the source within birth and death, one establishes the vow to sever evil and receives the *saṃvara-śīla* (the precepts of restraint);

by cultivating practices that counteract defilement, one proceeds toward the gate of non-action liberation (*anabhisaṃskāra-vimokṣa-mukha*) and realizes the Buddha of the Dharma-body through returning to original purity—this is called the "Virtue of Severance" (*prahāṇa-guṇa*).

Second, one establishes the vow to cultivate goodness and receives the *kuśala-dharma-saṃgrāhaka-śīla* (the precepts of gathering wholesome dharmas); by cultivating expedient practices, one proceeds toward the gate of emptiness liberation (*śūnyatā-vimokṣa-mukha*) and returns to one's original self-nature.

Upon realizing the *saṃbhogakāya* Buddha, it is called the "Virtue of Wisdom" (*jñāna-guṇa*). One establishes the vow to deliver sentient beings, receives the precepts for gathering and protecting them, cultivates practices of compassion, and proceeds toward the gate of signless liberation (*animitta-vimokṣamukha*) to realize the original state of equality, thereby attaining the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha, which is called the "Virtue of Grace" (*anugraha-guṇa*). It continues:
"In this turbid age, hindrances are deep and habitual tendencies are difficult to sever; those with a beginner's mind may be timid and prone to retreat from Bodhi."
Therefore, one must aspire to be born in the Pure Land of Amitābha. The three clusters of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*) are precisely the three grades of superior mind:

the restraint of conduct (*śīla*) is the sincere mind (*zhichengxin*); the cultivation of good and the practice of wisdom is the profound mind (*shenxin*); and the gathering of sentient beings for their benefit is the mind of dedication and aspiration (*huixiang fayuanxin*).
Once these three minds are possessed, one will certainly attain the superior grade and achieve the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*), without needing to wait for many [lifetimes].
To generate the Bodhi of the Buddha without any retreat or discouragement—this is the ultimate domain of the practitioner’s mind.

The commentary states that this is as explained elsewhere, namely what was cited above. Regarding the three practices being fully integrated, the first three phrases clarify that the mind must necessarily be accompanied by practice.
This is because the arousal of the mind is merely a hollow vow; one must fulfill that vow through practice. Therefore, it is said that [the mind] "must" [be accompanied by practice].
"Xiuran" (修然) means that although the latter two [stages] clarify practice (*caryā*), they do not encompass the mind (*citta*); the path is thus direct.

Although it is said to be "direct," one may cultivate practice without necessarily having generated the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*), yet one who practices must necessarily have generated that resolve; therefore, it is said that the meaning is complete.

Below, the three points indicate the scriptural text to verify that there are those who practice directly without generating the three resolves; hence it says, "furthermore, there are. This explains the three types of practice.

The *Sūtra on the Initial Practice* states: "As for those with a compassionate heart, because sentient beings commit slaughter due to their stubborn evil, one must now practice non-killing and necessarily give rise to a compassionate mind.

This precept is the discipline (*vinaya*) that severs evil; since one who can refrain from killing is necessarily able to uphold the precepts—and as the names of these precepts are general—they must be distinguished.
One must rely on the *Brahmajāla Sūtra* according to the Mahāyāna, rather than relying on the *Upāsaka-śīla Sūtra*, because...

The *Brahmajāla Sūtra* states that the reception [of precepts] encompasses both the gradual and the sudden, and benefits both monastics and laypeople; however, the "good precepts" (śīla) apply only to those who receive them gradually, thus restricting them to the monastic community.

It says: "If one wishes to receive the Bodhisattva precepts, one must first receive the five precepts, then the ten precepts, and finally the full ordination (*upasampadā*), after which one receives the Bodhisattva precepts.
This is like a four-story pagoda: it is impossible to reach the second story without passing through the first. And so forth.

Since it is appropriate for the four precepts to be received gradually, this accords with the scriptural references to "all precepts"; therefore, one relies upon them. Hereafter, the [precept] corresponding to the mind can be seen;
the other two follow this pattern. This *Xingjing* (Sutra on Practice) states: "Mahāyāna excludes the partial and small [vehicles];
'fang' (vast) refers to the teaching that expresses [the meaning], while 'deng' (equal) refers to the principle expressed, namely the vast and equal true reality (*bhūtatathatā*)."
Because its wondrous principle pervades all phenomena horizontally, it is called "Vaipulya" (Extensive); because it vertically encompasses both ordinary beings and sages, it is called "Equality.

Since the subsequent practice is identical to the preceding one, it is said that "it may be known. Regarding the statement that "one further adds the six mindfulnesses," the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm) states:
"Generally speaking, 'mindfulness' is a synonym for the internal mind’s act of retaining and recollecting. One focuses the mind..."

Because one recollects six types [of objects], it is called the "Six Recollections. Not only can they eliminate worldly fears, but they also remove all obstacles and difficulties of birth and death within the three realms.
1. Recollection of the Buddha: If one encounters terror or various obstacles and difficulties, one should recollect the Buddha’s immeasurable divine virtues.
Having recollected thus, fear and obstacles are immediately removed. 2. Recollection of the Dharma: The Buddha-dharma is subtle...

The Sangha of the Threefold Mindfulness is the disciple of the Buddha who has wondrously attained the fruits of the present life, is free from the burning of afflictions, is able to reach the excellent destination, and has attained unimpeded penetration;

they are endowed with the fivefold Dharma-body, consist of the four pairs and eight ranks, have attained the fruits of the three vehicles, are worthy of receiving offerings, and are the unsurpassed field of merit.
The mindfulness of the precepts is that which can obstruct all evils and is the dwelling place of peace and security. It is the precepts.

There are three kinds of restraint (*saṃvara*): that which is fixed (*niyata*), that which is associated with the Path (*mārga-sahagata*), and that which is capable of eliminating all evils of body and speech, obstructing the evil thoughts of the afflictions (*kleśa*), destroying ignorance (*avidyā*), and swiftly attaining liberation.
Regarding the "abandonment through the five recollections" (*pañca-smṛty-upāsana-tyāga*), there are two kinds of abandonment:
first, the abandonment of giving (*dāna-tyāga*), which can produce great merit; second, the abandonment of afflictions (*kleśa-tyāga*), by means of which one obtains wisdom and enters *parinirvāṇa*.

Regarding the six recollections of the devas (*ṣaḍ-devānusmṛti*): from the Heaven of the Four Great Kings up to the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations, there are further four types of devas—first, the worldly devas;
second, the birth devas; third, the pure devas; and fourth, the devas of meaning.

Thus, the *Fruition of Pure Benefit and Peace for All* (the *Miaozong*) quotes the *Commentary on the Nirvāṇa Sūtra*, which states: "The first three recollections concern others, while the latter three recollections concern oneself regarding precepts."
Generosity is its own cause; birth in heaven is its own fruit. Precepts are the goodness of cessation; generosity is the goodness of cultivation. Heaven has both proximate and remote fruits;

the remote is the heaven of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). Although the first three [refuges] involve others, if one realizes that the Three Jewels are of one essence and practices generosity and precepts with a single mind according to the principle of the ultimate truth, then one knows that among the six recollections, a single recollection is fully complete. This is what is called the Mahāyāna.
This distinguishes [the practice] from the six recollections (*ṣaḍ-anusmṛti*) of the Hīnayāna. Regarding the time limit, the first part correctly explains the scriptural text;
subsequently, it specifically clarifies the conditions for the response of one recollection, explaining the three sections as they appear in the text with great clarity.

In the section on "attaining birth," the first part explains "joyful exultation" (*pramuditā*), where "joy" arises from within the mind while "exultation" manifests in external deportment. Following the description of deportment, it explains "going."
Birth is like a cicada shedding its shell; this serves as a metaphor for the body remaining while the spirit departs. (End of section ten. Regarding the explanation of "a snap of the fingers":

although one travels ten trillion lands to the West in the time it takes to snap one's fingers, the reason for saying "a snap of the fingers" is explained by means of the power of the Buddha and the power of karma.

To say "as quick as turning over one’s hand" refers to the swiftness of attaining realization—what is called "attaining realization as easily as turning over one’s hand. However, the principle of the signs of rebirth is likewise difficult to clarify. (Beginning of section eleven.)
The sutra provides the analogy of a wax seal being pressed into clay: as the seal and the clay meet, the seal disappears and the impression is formed. This is used as a metaphor for ordinary beings:

when the aggregates (*skandhas*) of the present life cease, the aggregates of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) arise. By extension, this illustrates how for one who is reborn, the aggregates of this land cease and the aggregates of that land arise.
At the moment of death, one personally sees oneself seated upon a golden lotus; this is precisely the aggregate-body of birth in that land. Therefore, it is so.
The wise say that the mind abiding in meditative concentration at the moment of death is itself the Pure Land; a single movement of thought is the very time of being born in the Pure Land.
Only through direct realization of this state can one know that it is beyond description.

Generally speaking, when the power of one’s vows is firm and samādhi is mature, and furthermore, when one is embraced by the light and vows of Amitābha, one is naturally drawn there. This may be illustrated by analogy with the wholesome [karmic conditions].

Even if one were to fall into the three miserable realms or the four destinies, how could there be any conscious intent? It is solely because karma has ripened that one is involuntarily led to rebirth.

One need only believe the Buddha’s words and need not harbor doubts; this will bring benefit later on. Regarding the five signs within the middle section of the subsequent benefits, the initial, middle, and final stages differ from one another, as will be distinguished later by itself.
In the second stage, it is called "sublime" in contrast to the "coarse," manifesting that one has already set forth the Great [Vehicle] within the causal stage.
With the mind opened and great understanding attained, upon being born in that land, one hears the Great Dharma for the first time; thus, one is able to immediately awaken.

"Severance" refers to the destruction of ignorance, while "realization" refers to the manifestation of the *dharmatā*. The patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) encompasses everything from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Tiantai says that "patience of non-arising" refers to ascending to the first stage (*bhūmi*). The *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states it is the eighth stage.

Because the Bodhisattva personally realizes the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and enters the path of effortlessness (*anābhoga-mārga*), one knows that this stage of patience encompasses the longest duration of all positions;

it cannot be definitively delimited, but when judged by its meaning, it corresponds to the middle portion of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*). Having ascended to the stage of patience (*kṣānti-bhūmi*), he attains the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*);
therefore, in the space of a moment, he traverses various Buddha-fields. Among the four types of predictions (*vyākaraṇa*), there are both general and specific ones.
As various sutras state, "all shall attain the dharma-body of Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi" and so forth, these are general predictions (*sāmānya-vyākaraṇa*).

Alternatively, those that specify the name of the kalpa, the land, and the title [of the Buddha] are individual predictions (*viśeṣa-vyākaraṇa*) concerning the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). What is now called "bestowing the prediction" refers only to the general prediction. Among the five [categories], samādhi belongs to the nature of concentration (*samādhi-gotra*), while dhāraṇī belongs to the nature of wisdom (*prajñā-gotra*).

The commentary translates it as "total retention" (*saṃdhāraṇa*); six translations render it as "obstructing and retaining" (*vighna-dhāraṇa*), meaning to obstruct the evils of the two extremes and to retain [the wholesome].
Because the nature of the Middle Way’s excellent wisdom, once aroused, is unimpeded in all things, it is said that "infinite dharma-gates" and so forth are accessible.

Regarding the superior grade of birth through practice: the first point concerns the deficiency of goodness within the causal stage; the subsequent section provides the explanation for this initial point, which is the "Great Understanding.

Next is the "Great Mind," followed by "Faith," which is the "Great Faith," and then "Vow," according to the sequence of the sections. As for the term *hú* (fox), it refers to a sycophantic beast that constantly harbors hesitation.

This refers to the indecisiveness of the future, as stated in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*: "If I were to fully describe the merit of this sūtra, some who hear it would have their minds become deranged, filled with doubt, and fail to believe.

This is precisely what is meant. If one has not yet understood the ultimate principle (*paramārtha*), hearing of its profundity will surely cause fear, and hearing of its vastness will surely cause alarm;
such a person cannot avoid giving rise to slander. The three categories of causes and conditions can be understood through the following: the Golden Terrace is none other than the Lotus.
Regarding the "flower," according to the passage below, it blooms after one night has passed; thus, there is no doubt as to its meaning.

As for "attaining birth" in the middle and upper grades, since "a snap of the fingers" here corresponds to "a single thought-moment" (*ekacitta-kṣaṇa*), they are mentioned interchangeably. This is as seen in the Buddha’s own praise: "A single thought-moment brings one to the Treasure Realm;

a snap of the fingers allows one to gaze upon the Compassionate Countenance. It is precisely this that is being employed here. Regarding the nine sections on subsequent benefits, they are as stated in the text. Within the seventh [section], there is "non-retrogression."
Once one has been born in that land, from the stage of an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) until the attainment of Buddhahood, there is no further regression.
As stated in the *Ten Doubts Treatise* (*Shi yi lun*), this is because there are five causes and conditions by which all remain non-regressive;

yet, since it is here said that one "immediately attains non-regressive bodhi," why does the subsequent text further mention "attaining patience" (*kṣānti*) and "receiving a prediction" (*vyākaraṇa*)? One must understand that the previous mention of "non-regression" was made according to a general discourse on permanence.
Regarding the passage on "non-retrogression," it is only when one attains *kṣānti* (patience) that the actual realization is discussed. As for the single cycle of increase and decrease:
this refers to the period when the human lifespan increases by one year every hundred years from ten years up to eighty-four thousand years;
and from eighty-four thousand years, it decreases by one year every hundred years back down to ten years. This constitutes one intermediate kalpa (*antarakalpa*) of increase and decrease.

Regarding the causes for rebirth in the lower grade of the highest class (*śreṣṭha-adhimātra*), the correspondence between the presence or absence of the requisite conditions can be seen by comparing this with the Sūtra.

As for the lotus flower being the pedestal (*mañca-pīṭha*) within the conditions that induce rebirth: in the previous passage concerning the "Purple-Golden Pedestal," the commentary explained it as the lotus flower;

here, however, the "Golden Lotus Flower" is explained as the pedestal. Examining this, we know that although the Sūtra mentions the pedestal and the flower interchangeably, they are in fact one and the same, and thus one attains birth.

Regarding the section on "Benefits after [the Initial Attainment]" (*paścād-anuśaṃsa*), it may be understood by analogy with the preceding section on "Benefits before" (*pūrvānuśaṃsa*). The five segments within this section are explained according to the text.

In the *Śata-dharma-prakāśamukha-śāstra*, a passage from the *Daśabhūmika-parivarta* of the *Avataṃsaka-sūtra* is cited, stating that upon ascending to the first stage (*prathamā bhūmiḥ*), one becomes fully enlightened regarding all dharma-gates;
for each realization attained, a hundredfold manifestation occurs. The ten dharmas listed below are collectively acquired in a single kṣaṇa at the very beginning.

1. Through the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*), they clearly illuminate all phenomena; 2. they are able to see all Buddhas through and through, and further know their spiritual powers (*ṛddhibala*);
3. regarding the fourth, they are able to pass through and shake Buddha-fields; 4. regarding the fifth, wherever light shines, they can examine both the beginning and the end;

5. regarding the sixth, they teach and transform sentient beings; 6. they know the events of two eons (*kalpa*) within those [beings]; 7. in a single moment of thought, they suddenly enter the Dharma.
Regarding the nine gates, the one-many sovereignty, and the ten abilities to manifest retinues, the *Benevolent Kings Sūtra* speaks in terms of the progressive excellence of each stage (*bhūmi*).
In explaining the stages, "Joyful" (*pramuditā*) is so named because, having practiced through kalpas and newly ascended to the rank of the noble ones, one’s joy is beyond measure.
This concludes the summary and analysis of the five differences, wherein the commentary corresponds to the sūtra with such precision that not even a hair’s breadth of confusion exists.
In the fifteenth contemplation, the middle grade is presented as a whole; based on the sutra, the cultivation of causes and the resulting fruits are judged to belong to the Śrāvaka.

Furthermore, the *Aṣṭasāhasrikā-prajñāpāramitā* (Small Version) is cited to verify that this is not false. In the section resolving doubts, the text first clarifies the two types [of practitioners] in this land.

Regarding those of "fixed nature," their nature is already determined and can no longer be turned back; their bodhicitta has died out, they are indolent regarding the guidance of others, and they remain only where they are.
This refers to those who attained realization with haste at the Deer Park, cremated their bodies by fire, and entered the realm of nirvana without remainder (*anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇadhātu*).

Regarding the *Wangsheng lun* (Treatise on Rebirth), the *Miaozong chao* states: "The *Wuliangshou jing lun* (Treatise on the Sutra of Immeasurable Life) was composed by Vasubandhu and contains seventeen sections of accomplishment.
In the sixteenth section, 'Accomplishment of the Great Meaning Gate,' a verse says: 'The realm of Mahayana roots of goodness is beyond reproach...'"
Regarding the "names associated with women" and those who lack faculties, as well as those of the two vehicles who do not cultivate the seeds of practice, the *Vyākhyā* (Exegesis) states:

"Therefore, the retributive fruit of the Pure Land is free from the two kinds of faults of being censured: first, the substance (*tattva*), and second, the name (*nāman*). As for the substance, there are three [types of persons]:
first, those of the two vehicles; second, women; and third, those whose faculties are incomplete. Because these three kinds of faults are absent, it is called 'free from being censured.'"

It is also called "threefold," not merely in the sense that the three bodies do not exist, but even to the extent that the names of the two vehicles, women, and those with deficient faculties are not heard;
for these seventeen [categories] all clarify the retributive fruits of that land, and thus there are no [beings of] the two vehicles. The treatise states:
"Non-arising" refers to those of fixed nature (*niyata-gotra*). Those of unfixed nature (*aniyata-gotra*) are precisely those who turn their minds toward [the Mahāyāna].

Those who sat at the various assemblies during the Dali era heard the Mahayana Dharma and their minds gradually became clear and expansive; upon reaching the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, they obtained their prediction [of Buddhahood], and in the *Nirvāṇa*, they came to know the eternal.
Like Pūrṇa, they revealed their original ground and fundamental nature, manifesting the secret bodhisattva practices while appearing in the form of śrāvakas.
The intermediate words refer back to Śākyamuni’s original ground as the beginning, continuing directly until the present day of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.
Excluding the final [stage], all others belong to the intermediate [state]. For now, this text relies on a single period of transformative teaching:
after the Deer Park [turning of the wheel] and before the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*. It cannot be definitively pointed out that two sūtras serve as proof;

rather, it is shown that those śrāvakas who dwell in the Pure Land are precisely those who, at the end of their lives, resolve for the Great Mind and are then born in that land—exactly as it is here in this land.

The category of those with indeterminate nature is similar; however, the subsequent section resolves this doubt: "Since they have already aroused the great mind, why are they born there and further realize the Lesser Vehicle?

It is solely because they turn their minds back [to the Great Vehicle] that they attain rebirth there. It is solely because of their past habitual tendencies that they temporarily tread upon the provisional vehicle;

knowing the Great while realizing the Small, it is not considered ultimate. Therefore, it is said that they ultimately return [to the Great]. Using this case to illustrate the other is as clear as the bright sun.

Those with eyes should examine this (the rest is as in the *Fuxin*). To distinguish the redundant from the essential, it can be seen by comparing it with the sutra; making such a distinction beforehand prevents congestion when encountering the actual text.

In the *Sutra on Rebirth in the Middle Grade*, the introductory address is presented according to the text. Regarding the cultivation of causes and the clarification of practices, the first part provides a general indication of the sutra text:

"five and eight" refers specifically to the various precepts, while "precepts" generally refers to the Dharma; these encompass the tenfold complete precepts in terms of the Dharma, and refer to the person in terms of the individual.

It is called "all" (*sarva*) because it pertains to the five groups (*pañca-skandha*). The five [groups] are listed separately below. Regarding the two phrases concerning sexual misconduct (*kāma-mithyācāra*), they distinguish between the heterodox and the orthodox.
Regarding the *upavāsa* (fasting), the remaining names are explained and clarified; since the precepts are not the primary subject here, they are referred to as being according to the Vinaya.

The phrase "as follows" provides a general discussion of the common and specific aspects. The phrase "as below" points to the subsequent words in the sutra. Within the section on "wishes and aspirations," the sutra states, "by means of these roots of goodness," which refers specifically to the five [precepts].

Regarding the eight precepts: for this reason, the commentary marks them as causes, while those [precepts] produced from them are the effects. In reality, they have not yet arisen; this is spoken of in terms of the "aspirational mind" (*pranidhicitta*).

In the section on the conditions for the manifestation of the Dharma, it says that by practicing the four precepts, one attains access to both the monastic and the lay paths. The Sūtra states that it specifically extols leaving the household life (*pravrajyā*);

therefore, the commentary says that while it primarily gathers the monastic community, this is because the many are contrasted with the few, not that it excludes the laity. It further extols the four foundations of mindfulness (*smṛtyupasthāna*).

Because they rely on past habitual tendencies, when one is close [to the practice], it is governed by the boundaries of the precepts; when one is far [from the practice], it clarifies the Buddha’s original intent.

Since there are differences in the strength of the karmic retribution for men and women born within the Vinaya, there is a distinction between full kneeling (*jang-kwei*) and alternating kneeling (*hu-kwei*).

The scriptural text provides a general indication that differs from the Vinaya; subsequently, in China, the expansion and contraction [of the rites] varies, and those who have seen the Buddha should follow the preceding and following contexts.

It is verified that this is from the *Lüe wen fa* (Brief Exposition of the Dharma), which states: "Because one was habituated to studying the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) during the stage of the causal ground, it is said that one follows these habitual practices.

Tiantai says: "Suffering (*duḥkha*) involves the shifting of the three characteristics; accumulation (*samudaya*) involves the movement of the four minds; the Path (*mārga*) is easily subverted by its counteractives;

and cessation (*nirodha*) is the extinction of existence back into non-existence. The *Yi jiao* (Bequeathed Teachings) says: "The Buddha taught that the Truth of Suffering is truly suffering and cannot be made into pleasure; accumulation [is truly accumulation]..."

It is precisely because there is no other cause [for their cessation] than this that it is said they are all real; this refers to the four truths of arising and ceasing according to the Hīnayāna (etc.).

Regarding those who have attained the title of "Fruit of the Path" (*mārgaphala*) and whose "afflictions of the bonds are exhausted": because the "bondage of the seeds" (*bījabandhana*) of the three realms has been severed, they are "no longer subject to future existence" (*apunarbhava*);

because they are liberated from the "bondage of the fruits" (*phalabandhana*) of the three realms, these three names are as previously indicated among the three types of supernormal knowledge (*vidyā*) realized therein. These are the three names.
Regarding the fact that "clear knowledge" (*vidyā*) is also designated as "supernormal power" (*abhijñā*) while the other three are merely called "supernormal powers," the *Mahāvibhāṣā* states:
"The supernormal power of the body is merely craftsmanship; the divine ear is merely hearing sounds; and the knowledge of others' minds merely takes the distinct thoughts of others as its object.

Therefore, these are not 'clear knowledges. Only the knowledge of past lives produces great wearying detachment toward past suffering; the divine eye produces great wearying detachment toward future suffering; and the knowledge of the exhaustion of outflows [produces it] toward present suffering."

Because correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*) severs the afflictions (*kleśa*), these three are called "Great Treatises on Clarity" (*vidyā-mahā-śāstra*). Question: What is the distinction between "penetrating clarity" (*abhijñā*) and "clarity" (*vidyā*)?
Answer: Directly knowing the past and so forth is called "penetration"; knowing the causes, conditions, and karmic actions of the past and so forth is called "clarity.

Among the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍ-abhijñā*), the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*) and divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) refer to the attainment of the pure derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) of the form realm (*rūpa-dhātu*) while abiding in meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which then resides in the eyes and ears.
Regarding the ability to see and hear the sentient beings of the six realms as well as all the forms, colors, sounds, and thoughts of others within the faculties:

this refers to the arising of wisdom within meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that enables one to know the various mental activities and conditions of the minds of sentient beings in the six realms.

Regarding the knowledge of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*): this refers to the arising of wisdom within meditative concentration that enables one to know the past—one life, two lives, or up to a hundred—of oneself and others.

The supernormal power of recollecting past lives—spanning from ten million eons up to eighty thousand great kalpas—including the previous existences (*jātaka*) and the deeds performed therein (*itivṛttaka*), when accomplished at will, is also termed the supernormal power of the psychic realm (*ṛddhiviṣaya*).
This comprises two types: first, the ability to transform oneself, others, and all things in the world according to one’s will, which is the supernormal power of the psychic realm;
second, the ability to fly swiftly and reach destinations without obstruction by mountains or barriers.

This is precisely what is meant by "as one wishes. In the *Yingluo jing* (Sutra on Necklaces), it is called the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*). "Supernormal" (*shen*) refers to the celestial mind; "power" (*tong*) refers to the nature of wisdom.

Because this innate wisdom penetrates and illuminates all things without obstruction, it is called "supernormal power. As for the eight liberations (*aṣṭavimokṣa*), they are also called the eight renunciations (*aṣṭavaiśāradya*).

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states that they are all pure because one abandons the firm attachment to the five desires; thus, they are termed "renunciations" based on their cause, while they are termed "liberations" (*vimokṣa*) based on their result.

"Deliverance" (vimokṣa) is named after its fruit. Regarding "internal form": internal form refers to the skeletal body within one's own person, while external form refers to the four great elements and the six sense bases.
Because the fetters and proclivities of the desire realm are difficult to sever, one does not destroy the internal [body] but contemplates the external.

When this contemplation is perfected, one attains the stage of the first dhyāna; because one can relinquish both one’s own level and the lower desire realm, it is called "reversal and deliverance" (prātikūlya-vimokṣa). Second, by means of... [text continues].

Because of internal purity (*adhyātmasaṃprasāda*) in the second dhyāna, one does not dwell upon the internal image of the skeleton; furthermore, because the afflictions of desire are difficult to sever, one contemplates the external signs of impurity (*aśubha*).
Among these three objects of focus, one excludes the external sign of impurity and instead takes as the object the pure, brilliant, and luminous radiance produced within meditative concentration;
this is called "focusing on the pure body" (*śubhakāya*). Although the body experiences pleasure, the mind remains free from defilement.

The stage of "adherence" (*āśraya*) is situated within the four [formless attainments] of the third dhyāna; from the fourth [dhyāna] up to the seventh, they are collectively termed the "four emptinesses" (*catasraḥ śūnyatāḥ*).

This is because the essential nature of these four concentrations is devoid of form and color, and thus all are designated as "empty. Each takes its respective realized object as its basis (*āśraya*).

Because the objective phenomena sustain the mind and prevent it from scattering, they are called "concentration" (*samādhi*). First, one eliminates the fundamental matter (*rūpa*) of the fourth dhyāna and the three types of aversion.

Abandoning form and feeling aversion toward it as if it were a prison, one contemplates renunciation; when the mind accords with infinite space, this is called the Sphere of Infinite Space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*).
Since this meditative concentration arises based upon the aggregates, sense-bases, and elements, it is characterized by impermanence, suffering, emptiness, vanity, and unreality.

Consequently, the mind develops aversion and turns away from it, no longer experiencing attachment; thus, it is called "rejection" (*pratikūla-vairāgya*). Among these five [liberations], equanimity takes space as its object, while consciousness is the object of the [next] two.
Regarding the first [stage], because space is without boundary, when it becomes manifold, the mind scatters; thus one abandons space and turns the mind to take consciousness as its object.

The state in which the mind and consciousness are in mutual correspondence is called the *vijñānānantyāyatana-samādhi* (concentration of the sphere of infinite consciousness), and so forth. Regarding the sixth [stage], "abandoning consciousness" means that the consciousness of the three periods of time is likewise without limit;

if it becomes manifold through its objects, it can disrupt the concentration, so one must abandon it once more and take non-existence (*akiṃcanya*) as the object, and so forth. Regarding the seventh [stage]...
The practitioner becomes weary of the sphere of nothingness as being like a state of delusion, and views the sphere of perception as being like a festering ulcer.

By taking the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception as an object, they enter meditative absorption; because the mind is unified with this concentration, it is called "neither-perception-nor-non-perception.

Some say that when ordinary people and non-Buddhists attain this concentration, they are said to have realized *nirvāṇa* and severed all perceptions, and thus it is called "neither-perception"; however, for the disciples of the Buddha, it is not so.
Because one knows as it truly is that there exists a subtle perception (*sūkṣma-saṃjñā*) which abides based on the four assemblies, it is said that this is not "non-perception" (*asaṃjñin*);

thus, this name is established by combining both its attainment and its loss. One thereby knows that this meditative concentration is cultivated by both ordinary people and non-Buddhists alike. Among the eight [liberations], it is also called "cessation-nirvāṇa" (*nirodha-nirvāṇa*). Regarding the phrase "extinguishing feeling and perception" (*vedanā-saṃjñā-vyupaśama*), "feeling" (*vedanā*)...

Regarding "anticipating their intentions and fulfilling their aspirations": the *Liji* (Book of Rites), in the section attributed to Zengzi, states, "What we call filial piety in a gentleman is anticipating their intentions and fulfilling their aspirations, thereby instructing his parents in the Way.

Regarding benevolence (*ren*), it is said that one "extends love to all things. The phrase "broadly bestowing and rescuing the multitude" also originates from the *Analects*.

If even Yao and Shun were concerned about the difficulty of this, how much more so for others? The final two lines of the Confucian master’s [text] conclude by establishing benevolence and compassion as virtue.
The saying goes: "If one day you can overcome yourself and return to ritual propriety (*li*), the whole world will turn to benevolence.

Those who encounter such an opportunity do so because they have cultivated the roots of goodness—filial piety, nourishing parents, benevolence, and compassion—during their ordinary days; thus, at the moment of death, they meet with the favorable condition of encountering a spiritual teacher (*kalyāṇamitra*).

Regarding this "encountering the opportunity," first the name of the spiritual teacher is explained as "Dharma" (*fa*), followed by a citation from the sutras as proof. Below this, it is shown that this is not restricted to a single country, and below that, the joyful matters are explained.

As for those who are "vague" (*fan’er*), this refers to those who are indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and lax, as there are interruptions during the three periods [of the day].

The name of the Buddha is the result of cultivation over many kalpas; it encompasses his myriad virtues and is manifested in these four characters.

they are not the primary subject here, so I shall be brief. The scriptural citations following this passage are from the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*. It is not necessarily the case that stealing monastic property is more grave than the five heinous crimes (*pañcānantarya*); this is according to the scripture.

They bite one another. When encountering conditions, the fire is itself one, yet it is called "multitudinous" because it differs according to the vessel.

"The pure land is adorned by the forty-eight vows; with its lotus ponds and jeweled trees, it is easy to go to, yet no one goes. Fire.

Good and evil causes and effects are entirely one's own mind and nothing else; what is called "a non-human spirit burning you" is actually your own self-burning.

To destroy delusion by taking the fruit from its cause is precisely what constitutes liberation (*vimukti*). Tiantai says that liberation is the gate to *nirvāṇa*;

Because this is the opposite of the present [view], it must be decisively clarified. In the initial section of the current exposition, the impartiality of the power of vows is generally described;
in the following two sections, the essential nature of the vows of all Buddhas is specifically demonstrated as being pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.

If even benevolent men and gentlemen would not dare to do such a thing, how much less so the Buddha-mind? Master Xiachuan said:
"Both passages employ the inferior to illustrate the superior, thereby revealing the profound power of Amitābha’s vows. This concludes the first section on "Showing What is Included and Excluded."

The phrase "clarifying that [they] are excluded" refers to the fact that because that sutra seeks to manifest the supreme excellence of the realm of Ultimate Bliss, those beings who are born there are without exception purely virtuous companions;
how could those who harbor perverse slander be permitted to participate?

The intent is to exhort sentient beings of the末代 (final age) to transform their goodness and reform their evils, and to aspire to ascend upon the company of the superior sages. The subsequent phrase clarifies what is now being accepted.
This is likely because the pure karma discussed in the present sutra is precisely the ultimate Dharma of the One Buddha Vehicle;

that "it is this mind that makes the Buddha" and "this mind is the Buddha" originates from this very sutra, which is identical to the *Lotus Sūtra*’s revelation of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—a definitive, sudden teaching beyond which there is nothing superior.
Provided one can, for even a single thought-moment, dedicate [one's merit] with the vow to extinguish karma and break through obstacles, there is no need for further exertion.
If one were to cause perverse slanders not to arise, how would this differ from the partial and expedient teachings that lack full understanding?

Therefore, the suppression of the former and the exaltation of the latter are nothing other than means to transform sentient beings; thus, while the two sutras differ in their selection and inclusion, it is said that "the words deviate from the Buddha’s intent" because there is no partiality regarding good and evil, and "the ultimate aim accords" because both texts reach the same conclusion.
These last two phrases together conclude the discussion of the two sutras (this is a brief commentary on the text; for further details, see the *Fuxin*, where they are fully analyzed).
In the citation of scriptural evidence, since this sutra specifically clarifies the Samādhi of Contemplating the Buddha, it is appropriate to cite that [other scripture] as corroborative proof.
First, the primary citation—from "one day and one night" up to "one mark and one excellence"—cites a small portion to illustrate the greater, thereby manifesting the superiority of its merit.

The following two lines conclude by demonstrating the retribution. Although the preceding text mentions the five heinous crimes, they need not necessarily all be present; therefore, it says "according to."

The *Fanjing* (Sutra on Transgressions) states that those who undergo suffering do so "without end. In Sanskrit, this is *kalpa*, translated as "innumerable time. If even a single *kalpa* is thus, how much more so many *kalpas*?
Furthermore, to speak of the general outline of the number of *kalpas*: if one considers the karma of the mind, it is evident they are infinite.

Even the initial stage of encountering conditions is due to seeds from past lives; thus, upon meeting a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) who preaches the Dharma and teaches mindfulness, [the practice] is thereby brought forth.
Fearing that it might be interpreted as merely producing sound, [the commentator] explains the character "nian" (念) in the sutra through visualization.

When the afflictions of illness manifest as the emergence of evil karma, one is subsequently beset by various miseries; with the mental consciousness thus becoming desolate and bewildered, how could one possibly perform visualization?

Regarding the practice of ten recitations, one should simply be neither too slow nor too hurried, following the natural length of the breath without limiting the number of Buddhas. (As stated at length: Now, at this moment of death, time is so urgent and pressing;

The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* contains this inquiry: although this mind lasts but a short time, its power is fierce and sharp, like that of one on the verge of death.
