"That which arises through conditions has no intrinsic nature. The *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā* states: "All phenomena do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from another, nor from both, nor without a cause. Therefore..."

It is said that non-arising transcends the four modes of being (*catuskoṭi*) and cuts off the hundred negations; therefore, it is called "naturelessness. This nature of naturelessness is itself the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

The first line of the verse from the *Caryā-dharmapada-sūtra* clarifies the characteristics of sinful karma: since the karma created therein encompasses the three obstructions (*trividha-āvaraṇa*), it is said to "completely obscure" them.
Because it covers the three virtues, it is termed an "obstruction" (*āvaraṇa*). Being profound, vast, and boundless, it is metaphorically compared to the ocean.

The second line concerns the mental karma that creates [rebirth]; since it lacks intrinsic nature, one fails to realize through deluded conceptualization that the fundamental nature of all phenomena is empty and quiescent, and thus takes objects with the mind, thereby creating deluded karma.

The latter half clarifies the method of repentance (*pāpadeśanā*): the first phrase seeks the capacity [of the practitioner], while the second phrase correctly explains sitting upright as the manifestation of physical deportment.
"Mindfulness" refers to the wisdom of the contemplator, and "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*) refers to the object of contemplation.

Since one has already realized that all dharmas are none other than the true mark (*dharmatā*), what transgression would not be eliminated? Yet, since the true mark is itself without characteristics (*animitta*), how should one maintain mindfulness?
One should know that by means of "mindfulness without mindfulness," one mindfully contemplates the markless mark; by means of the markless mark, one accords with mindfulness without mindfulness.

If one were to think that there are marks external to mindfulness, or that there is mindfulness external to marks, then this is not the Mahāyāna mindfulness of the true mark. This concludes the three-part analysis.
The causal practice leading to entry into realization and the vision of the Buddha can be understood by consulting the sutras.

Regarding the third section of the main body (*zhengzong*), which reveals the benefits and provides a concluding exhortation: first, it correctly clarifies that the assembly has witnessed [the vision].

Below this, in contrast with what precedes it, it distinguishes those who previously saw [the Buddha] alone; these refer to the beginning of the main body and the "Contemplation of the Lotus Throne" (*huazuo guan*). Now, below this, it further points out the present text.
The Sūtra states: "When these words were spoken, and when [the beings] heard what the Buddha taught"—this refers generally to the sixteen contemplation methods (*ṣoḍaśa-vipaśyanā*).

Regarding the attainment of benefits, the first section describes "pervasive penetration" (the character *huō* is pronounced *hù guā*) as a state of thorough realization. "Destroying ignorance" (*avidyā*) is explained in terms of the act of destruction itself.

"Realizing the dharma-nature" (*dharmatā*) is stated from the perspective of the principle realized; if one refers instead to the stage of attainment, it corresponds to the first *bhūmi* (the Stage of Initial Abiding).
A beginner practitioner who, upon hearing the sixteen contemplations, practices them accordingly and personally beholds the adornments of the environment and inhabitants of that land;
furthermore, hearing that "the mind creates" and "the mind is," they realize that all phenomena are interpenetrating and that there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm.

When the capacity for the Mahayana is thus aroused, they suddenly shatter ignorance and immediately enter the perfect stage; this is why it is called "sudden enlightenment" (*haoran*). This is from the first section on the Attendant Maidens.

Because one contemplates according to what has been heard, the great mind is awakened and perfumed; one records the aspiration for rebirth there, and only then does the treatise discuss the progressive cultivation and the entry into realization.
This section on dispelling doubts is as previously cited in the initial direct response among the answers. Below are two segments of supporting evidence:

the first proves that there are no women, and the second proves that there are no deficiencies of sense organs. This concludes by clarifying the *Ten Doubts Treatise*, which is the [first]... [of the ten].
Regarding Mount Jiuyi, the *Tiantai Shu* states: "The treatise says that women whose faculties are deficient are not reborn; this is said in reference to them.

Because the sutra speaks of those who first go [to the Pure Land], all those with wholesome minds attain rebirth. As for those among the devas who have resolved their minds, this refers to the assembly gathered at the 'Mysterious Palace' (the womb-palace) who heard the teaching together.
The scriptural text merely cites Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas raining flowers and following along as they hear the Dharma and resolve their minds."
This was personally recorded by the author while awaiting the Buddha’s return to the mountain; it shall be further elaborated upon later.

Regarding the third major section, the Dissemination (*Pravāraṇā*), this is the initial heading within the discourse itself, as can be seen from the division of the text; the subsequent commentary follows this first rubric.

The "double question" refers to the passage beginning with "At that time, Ānanda... and so forth. As for the answer concerning the name of the scripture, it is all as explained [in the preceding commentary].

Having already distinguished the maintenance of the teaching within the title, one knows that it is not received without faith and not maintained without mindfulness. When the power of faith and mindfulness is strong, how could there be any forgetfulness?
Regarding the exhortation to practice within the section on "Seeing the Realm," recollecting the Buddha and mindful of the Buddha is precisely what this sutra means by practicing this samādhi.

As for "manifesting the body" based on the cause and "extinguishing transgressions" regarding the future fruit, the sutra states: "To recollect is to contemplate. *Note: IAST diacritics have been used for Sanskrit terms (e.g., samādhi) as requested.*

Regarding the first of the three excellences of the body (*kāya-viśeṣa*), the names are presented first and their meanings follow. Because white is the fundamental color among all colors, it is called a "rare and auspicious" sign;
yet because it is not defiled even when born from the mud, it is said to be "pure by nature. The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "Among the flowers born in water, the *puṇḍarīka* is the foremost.
For those who practice the recollection of the Buddha (*buddhānusmṛti*), there is no peer; thus, these two [the white lotus and the recollection of the Buddha] are preeminent among excellences.

The Great Being occupies the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), and is therefore called "one in the final birth" (*ekajātipratibaddha*). Since he has cultivated *samādhi* and nurtured the holy embryo (*āryagarbha*), his nature and category are identical [to those of the Buddhas], and thus he becomes their companion.
Regarding the superior retribution, the first [point] explains "sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*) by means of attaining Buddhahood;

the second explains the name "site of enlightenment"; the third explains the power of the family of all Buddhas; and the fourth cites two sūtras as proof that he is not far from the Buddhas. This proves [the point].
Above, one shall sit at the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*), never regressing from *bodhi*, and realize rebirth into the family of the Buddhas.

The Buddhas manifest their response by necessarily possessing the eight phases (*aṣṭa-lakṣaṇa*): descending from Tuṣita, entering the womb, being born, leaving the city, subduing Māra, attaining enlightenment, preaching the Dharma, and entering *parinirvāṇa*.
This text summarizes these principles; in truth, they must all be complete. One seeks to go to the Pure Land of Amitābha; as the Sūtra says: "To be born..."
Because they belong to the family of all Buddhas, this is explained by means of the single essence of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Regarding the phrase "you who are good" in the *Zhongjing* (Middle Sutra), it is intended to inspire reverence and prevent arrogance. It instructs the reciter to compare the two modes of upholding: the upholding of the name and the upholding of the sutra.
Although the names are few and the scriptural text is extensive, if one can remember and maintain them, their merit is equal.
This is intended to manifest that the merit of holding the Name is great; why is this so?

It is because the four-character name of Amitābha has been adorned by immeasurable practices and vows cultivated throughout kalpas from cause to fruition. To raise a thought and recite it once is to possess all myriad virtues;
moreover, the sixteen wondrous realms and the two-fold retribution of the environment and inhabitants described in the sutra are likewise due to the vows of Amitābha.

Because it is accomplished through power, one knows that upholding the name and upholding the sutra are equal. Among the various forms of joy, the commentary explains the "great" in the phrase "great sutra" through three meanings.
If the Buddha did not speak [of this land], how could it be heard? Since even hearing it is not easy, how much more so is being born there?
These two constitute self-benefit. The formal request made by the Great Skillful Means (Mahā-upāya) is precisely for the sake of future self-benefit and the benefit of others.

The original intention is finally fulfilled, and no meaning of "great joy" exceeds this. Regarding the first section within the two turnings of the teaching, the identity of the audience is difficult to determine;

therefore, it is illustrated by means of two principles. Second, as for the repeated exhortations shown in the actual turning of the teaching, according to the preceding scriptural text, there are four instances:
first, after the three blessings; second, within the contemplation of the stages; third, at the beginning of the lotus seat; and fourth, [at the beginning of the chapter on the parable].

This is precisely what was repeatedly entrusted in the previous chapter, with the intent that [the teaching] be returned to the mountains to be further expounded; this is the meaning of the Buddha’s intention here.
When the assembly dispersed, this was the occasion for the re-exposition at Vulture Peak (*Gṛdhrakūṭa*). Thus, it can be compared with the previous version to discern its breadth and brevity.

Furthermore, it is pointed out that Ānanda acted as a spokesperson, whereby these words may be called the Buddha’s own teaching. Having possessed even a hair’s breadth of goodness in the past, one has now encountered the gateway to Right Contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). New.
This commentary has been widely circulated to directly reveal the path to rebirth in the Pure Land.

I now offer this brief praise and exposition, like a speck of dust or a drop of dew before the mountains and oceans, universally dedicating it to all sentient beings with a vow that reaches to the end of the future: may we all be born together in the Land of Peaceful Nurturing (Sukhāvatī).
May the seeds of merit from the destruction or praise of this commentary and record become the cause for all Buddhas to grant their secret empowerment, so that benefit may be inexhaustible.
